## On a receiver card the joint that fails is a ribbon header, three years later, on a wall nobody can reach

Source: https://tenmaypcba.com/insights/led-receiver-card-ribbon-headers.html
Published: 2026-11-19
Summary: A cabinet card is cheap, long, and covered in headers that get cycled during install. Why the connector and the through-hole fill decide the field failure, not the placement.

An LED display is a wall of identical cabinets, each with one or more receiver cards and a sender card upstream. The receiver card is long and narrow, usually with eight or more ribbon headers along its edge feeding hub boards, and it is ordered in thousands because the wall is measured in square metres.

The card is simple and cheap. That is exactly the problem: on a part this cheap, the only visible variable is price, and the only invisible variable is the process — which is why the failure this family produces is almost always the same one.

### Eight headers, and every one of them is a lever

A ribbon header is a mechanical interface that gets mated during installation, possibly re-mated during service, and then left for years. Three things about it are decided at build:

- Through-hole fill. These are through-hole parts on a thin board. Insufficient fill gives a joint that survives the factory and cracks on the third installation.
- Header seating and coplanarity. A header that is a fraction off-square puts the ribbon under tension, and the tension lands on the solder joints at both ends.
- Handing during packing. Long thin boards flex. A card that is packed with the headers taking the load arrives pre-stressed.

An AOI pass rate says nothing about any of those three. A pull test on the first article and a written seating method do.

### This family is priced in cents and ordered in thousands

At 1,000 to 10,000 pcs, the economics are dominated by material and yield, not by setup. Which changes the honest advice: the lever here is not negotiation, it is the panel design and the process stability.

- Panelisation matters more than on any other family. Long boards with a high header count want a panel that carries them flat through reflow and depanelisation.
- One stencil revision, held. A card that is re-tooled between batches at this price point is a batch that will differ.
- Coating, if specified, is a cost you should interrogate. Outdoor cabinets usually want it; indoor rental walls often do not. Coating eight headers correctly means masking eight headers, and that labour is real.

The cent-per-board argument is worth reading before you buy on price: how to tell whether an LED driver quote is real (/insights/led-driver-quote-reality-check.html) makes the same case one step upstream in the same industry.

### What is not measured here: the colour, the wall, the EMC

Nothing on this floor produces a picture. Specifically not available:

- Colour, brightness, gamma or refresh calibration at cabinet level, and any pixel-level or wall-level test.
- EMC pre-compliance or compliance testing, ingress (IP) testing, salt-fog and UV ageing of the cabinet.
- Cabinet mechanical assembly, power-supply integration, front-face lamination.
- Any end-to-end proof that the finished screen works before it ships.

So the acceptance plan is yours: a test jig on the hub interface, a burn-in rack, and a cabinet-level visual check at the integrator. That is normal for this industry — but it means the assembler is being bought for consistency, not for proof.

### Where the board stops and somebody else starts

A clean split looks like this: the card is assembled, inspected, and recorded here; the cabinet is built, powered, sealed and calibrated by the cabinet maker; the wall is commissioned on site with the control system. Almost every dispute in this product category comes from one of those three steps being assumed by the wrong party.

### What to send for a quote

Gerber with the panelisation, the stack-up, the BOM, the centroid, the header list with the seating and pull requirements, the coating and mask drawing if any, and the quantity with the variant count. At 1,000 to 10,000 pcs the build is three working days from kitted parts, and the through-hole operation is the rate limiter.

The family page is LED display control and receiver cards (/applications/led-display.html). For the coating-versus-cost argument in this industry, the LED driver quote reality check (/insights/led-driver-quote-reality-check.html); for where a cheap board stops being cheap, what is inside a PCBA price (/insights/pcba-cost-per-board.html).

## On a medical device the board is ordinary and the record is not

Source: https://tenmaypcba.com/insights/medical-board-ordinary-record-is-not.html
Published: 2026-11-19
Summary: Acquisition, main and UI boards in a device that lives a decade. Why the assembly question is about documents and revisions rather than about placement.

Of all the families on this site, medical is the one where the assembly is least interesting and the paperwork is most. A patient monitor or a diagnostic instrument carries two or three boards: an acquisition board with a guarded analogue front end, a main board, and a UI or panel board. Fine pitch, sometimes BGA, sometimes a guarded ring on the analogue side. Most competent lines can build it.

What most lines cannot do is answer a question two years later about which lot a serial came from, and that is the question a medical programme is actually buying.

### What this floor can be to a device maker

The honest description is: a competent contract assembler with ISO 9001:2015, working to your drawings, with a per-lot record you can retrieve. That is a real and useful role for a device company that owns its design, its firmware, its clinical validation and its regulatory submission.

What it is not is a medical-certified manufacturer. ISO 13485 is not held here, and neither is the quality-system audit trail that comes with it. A device that needs its contract manufacturer inside the QMS scope needs a different counterpart, and finding that out during an audit is expensive.

### Cleanliness and guarding: where assembly changes the reading

The analogue front end on an acquisition board is guarded for a reason, and three assembly habits quietly defeat the guard:

- Flux and residue across the guard ring. No-clean processes are fine when they are consistently no-clean; a repair with activated flux that is never washed is not.
- Coating bridging a guarded area. The mask list is not optional on this family. Coat the ring and the leakage number moves.
- Handling. Boards that sit open on a bench pick up what the room contains, and this family is low volume, so they sit longer.

None of those shows up as a failure at inspection. They show up as a channel that drifts, and then as a service visit.

### A lot record that survives a question two years later

The record set worth agreeing in writing, because it is what a medical customer asks for:

- First-article photographs and the drawing revision they were built to
- SPI results before reflow and AOI results after, filed per lot rather than summarised
- X-ray images for BGA and any guarded-joint area, per lot
- The coating record with the mask list used
- Traceability from lot to the component date codes that went in

A record that exists is worth a great deal in a complaint. A record that was summarised into a pass percentage is worth nothing, because it cannot answer the only question being asked.

### A device lives for a decade; the BOM does not

Medical instruments stay in service far longer than the parts inside them stay in production. The substitution question therefore arrives on every programme sooner or later, and it needs a written process rather than a phone call: who may propose an alternate, what evidence comes with it, who signs, and whether the change requires re-verification on your side.

That process is worth more than a lower unit price, and it is the point where a supplier who is honest about lifecycle becomes cheaper than one who is simply cheap.

### Where this floor stops

- ISO 13485 certification and any QMS audit trail under it. Not held.
- Sterilisation, biocompatibility and packaging validation, and the regulatory submission itself.
- In-circuit or functional test of the finished device, and any test that touches patient safety.
- Volumes in the tens of thousands a year, where a medical-certified contract manufacturer is the right counterpart.

### What to send for a quote

Gerber with the stack-up and the guarding drawing, the BOM, the centroid, the coating and mask list including guarded areas, the record set you require, the substitution policy you want followed, and the quantity. At 100 to 1,000 sets the build is three working days from kitted parts.

The family page is medical device and diagnostic instrument boards (/applications/medical.html). For the same argument applied to another certified industry, do you need IATF 16949 for an aftermarket part (/insights/no-iatf-16949.html); for what inspection actually proves, what AOI and X-ray can and cannot catch (/insights/what-aoi-xray-cannot-catch.html).

## An off-highway controller is judged in a field six months after it left the line

Source: https://tenmaypcba.com/insights/off-highway-coating-in-a-casting.html
Published: 2026-11-19
Summary: One or two boards per machine, coated, with valve drivers on the logic side and load dump on the power side. Where the build risk sits before the machine is ever driven.

A tractor or excavator controller is one or two boards inside a sealed cast aluminium housing bolted to a frame. It drives hydraulic valve solenoids, reads sensors, talks over CAN, and lives in dust, vibration, and a temperature range that a sealed casting makes worse rather than better.

It is also the family where the gap between what assembly can prove and what the machine will experience is widest. That gap is not a defect; it is a boundary, and buyers who know where it sits make better decisions about price.

### Coating is not a finish on this family, it is the product

Every board here is conformal coated, and the coating is doing real work: condensation, dust, oil mist and the occasional pressure wash nearby.

What that requires is a specification rather than a bottle:

- Mask list. Sealed connector pins, test points, pressure-sensitive sensors, and any surface that must stay conductive. A coated connector pin is a fault that appears as a communication error on a cold morning.
- Material and thickness. Polyurethane and silicone behave differently on thermal cycling; the callout should name one and say how the film is checked.
- Cure before handling. Coated boards that are handled wet lose the coating exactly where the harness lands.
- Rework sequence. Cut back, repair, re-coat, and record it. A reworked board without re-coating is a board with a hole in its protection.

The rest of the family follows from this: a coated board forces you to think about what is masked, and what is masked forces you to think about what the housing has to seal.

### Valve current, load dump, and the joints that carry both

The power side is heavy copper driving inductive loads, and the failure modes are the classic ones:

Risk: Where it is decided · What inspection proves
Voiding under the FETs: Paste volume, reflow profile · X-ray on the power joints, per lot
Solder fill on valve driver tabs: Through-hole method, thermal mass · First-article pull and cross-section
Coating bridging the isolation gap: Mask drawing, coating method · Visual under magnification, photographed
Connector strain: Connector choice, board edge design · Nothing — it is a design decision

That last row is the honest one. Some of the most important decisions on this family cannot be inspected at all, because they were made on the drawing.

### What is not proven here: sealing, EMC, vibration, functional safety

The list is long and it is worth stating without softening:

- No ingress (IP) testing, no burst or leak-down test of the sealed casting, and therefore no IP rating for the finished controller.
- No EMC, load-dump, vibration, thermal-shock or salt-spray qualification, and no certified test report.
- No functional safety certification — ISO 13849, IEC 61508, any PL or SIL claim — and no IATF 16949 work as a Tier supplier.
- No hydraulic valve calibration or end-of-line actuator test.
- No potting or encapsulation of the board. Coating is what this floor does.

A machine programme that needs any of those is not being badly served by this floor; it is being served by the wrong party for those steps, which is a different and more fixable problem.

### A hundred machines is a normal order, and it stays a hundred

At 100 to 1,000 sets, this is a long-life, low-volume, revision-light family — the opposite of a consumer product. The right supplier is one whose process does not drift between orders two years apart, and whose record lets you prove it did not.

That is why the useful question at quotation is not "what is your price at 500" but "what does your record look like, and can I have the first-article pack from the last time you built this".

### What to send for a quote

Gerber with copper weights and the stack-up, the BOM including the load-dump and protection parts, the centroid, the sealed connector list with the mating half and pin assignment, the coating and mask drawing with the isolation gap marked, the valve driver joint callout, and the quantity. At 100 to 1,000 sets a build is three working days from kitted parts.

The family page is off-highway and agricultural controllers (/applications/off-highway.html). For the similar coating argument in a handheld, where the coating is the product (/insights/rugged-radio-coating-is-the-product.html); for the certification question in automotive work, do you need IATF 16949 (/insights/no-iatf-16949.html).

## A payment terminal has one trace that must never be nicked, and nothing here can prove it survived

Source: https://tenmaypcba.com/insights/payment-terminal-tamper-mesh.html
Published: 2026-11-19
Summary: Two to four boards per terminal, one of them wrapped in a mesh whose failure is silent. Why the audit should come before the price, and who owns provisioning.

A payment terminal is two to four boards: a main board, a keypad and reader board, a printer board, sometimes a display board. On the main board there is a tamper detection mesh — a fine, dense, deliberate pattern of traces whose whole purpose is to break in a way the secure element can detect.

That mesh turns an ordinary assembly job into one with a single catastrophic failure mode that leaves no symptom at inspection. Which is why the security conversation belongs at the start of the programme rather than in the last week before certification.

### Start with the audit, because the buyer will

A terminal buyer eventually gets audited, and the audit reaches the manufacturing chain. What it looks for is not a claim of capability but evidence of control: who handled the boards, what the process was, what records exist, and what happens when a board fails.

Two things are true and both need saying early:

- This floor is not inside a payment-security certification. No PCI PTS approval, no EMVCo test report, no scheme audit, no secure facility.
- This floor can build and record boards to a drawing, including the mesh as an assembly feature, with per-lot traceability.

A programme that needs its manufacturer inside the security scope needs a different counterpart. A programme that needs boards built and recorded, with security verification on your side, is a fit — provided that split is agreed in writing.

### The tamper mesh is an assembly feature before it is a security feature

The mesh is inspected as a physical feature here: continuity of the pattern, no scratch, no solder splash, no coating bridging two traces that must stay separate.

Three process realities:

- Coating over a mesh is a decision, not a default. Coating can protect the mesh mechanically; it can also hide a bridge until the secure element reports tampering, at which point the unit is scrap.
- Rework near the mesh is close to forbidden. A board that needs rework inside the mesh area is usually a board that should be scrapped, and the process should say so rather than leaving it to judgement at the station.
- Handling. A dense fine-pitch board with a mesh on it does not want to be stacked, slid or squeezed, and at 500 to 5,000 pieces there are plenty of opportunities.

Continuity testing of the mesh is yours. This floor can inspect it as a feature and photograph it; it cannot tell you whether the detection circuit behaves.

### Secure-element provisioning and key injection

The question that stops programmes is who holds the key material. It is not a manufacturing preference; it is a security architecture decision with a certificate attached.

The rule that works: decide it in writing before the first build, never add it mid-run. If key injection happens at a party that holds the key material, the boards ship uninjected and the process after that belongs to them. If it happens here, the process, the environment and the audit trail all have to be agreed first — and this floor does not provision secure elements as a standard build step.

The same reasoning applies to card-reader function: magstripe, contact and contactless reads are not exercised here. There is no in-circuit test and no functional test, so the first time a card is tapped is at your bench. That is workable; assuming otherwise is not.

### The parts that get abused: printer, keypad, card slot

Terminals are handled by the public, all day. The board-level consequences are mechanical:

- Keypad and reader board joints take repeated force; through-hole and reinforced pads are drawing decisions.
- The card slot is a lever into the housing; the board behind it should not be the thing limiting insertion depth.
- The printer assembly is the highest-cycle mechanism in the product and is usually its own board for exactly that reason.

### Where this floor stops

- Tamper-mesh continuity, tamper response and key destruction. Verified by you with the secure element in place.
- Any payment-scheme approval or test, and any secure facility.
- Secure-element provisioning and key injection as a standard step.
- Card-reader function of any kind, and any in-circuit or functional test.
- Drop, ingress and EMC testing, and sitting inside the security certification scope.

### What to send for a quote

Gerber with the stack-up, the BOM with the secure element named, the centroid, the mesh drawing and the mask list, the keypad and reader connector list, the printer interface, and the quantity plus the variant matrix. At 500 to 5,000 pcs a build is three working days from kitted parts.

The family page is POS and payment terminal boards (/applications/pos-terminal.html). For how the manufacturing audit actually runs, how to audit a PCBA supplier without visiting (/insights/pcba-supplier-audit-checklist.html); for the test question, what to do when your assembler has no in-circuit test (/insights/in-circuit-test-outsourcing.html).

## The motor tabs on a power tool controller are soldered, and that is the whole job

Source: https://tenmaypcba.com/insights/power-tool-motor-tabs-soldered.html
Published: 2026-11-19
Summary: One or two boards, thousands of identical pieces, and a joint carrying twenty amps inside a sealed handle. Why the through-hole tabs and the coating decide field life.

A brushless tool controller is a power board that lives inside a handle. No fan, no airflow, no service access, and a user who will run it until the battery is flat and then put it down hot. The circuit is a three-phase bridge, a gate driver, current sense and a microcontroller that reads a trigger. Simple.

What is not simple is that the board's two hardest joints are the ones carrying the motor current, and they are made by hand or by selective solder rather than by the placer. On a tool, the assembly's job is those joints, the coating, and the fact that there are five thousand of them.

### A power board, not a computing board

Two or three ounces of copper on the power side, a heavy-copper bridge under a heatsink or a potted block, and a control section that could fit on a fingernail. Everything about the build follows from that split:

- The bridge needs a documented reflow profile. Heavy copper on one side and fine traces on the other is a compromise, and a profile borrowed from another board is a latent void.
- Voiding under the FETs is the yield number. Not the placement count, not the AOI pass rate. A voided joint on a 20 A bridge is a device that runs hot and derates in the user's hand.
- The heatsink interface is mechanical. Pad or paste, flatness, and the torque on the mounting screws. All three belong on the drawing.

### The motor tabs are soldered, not placed

The motor connects to the board through tabs or a terminal block, and that joint carries the full phase current. It is through-hole, it is thermally massive, and it is done in-house here by selective or hand solder with the joint specified and inspected.

Three failure modes are worth naming because none of them shows up on an AOI screen:

- Insufficient fill. Looks soldered, measures cold, heats under load, fails in month four.
- Cold joint on a plated tab. No amount of flux fixes a surface that will not wet; it needs the plating and the paste to be compatible.
- Mechanical load applied to the joint. If the tab is also the mounting point, the solder is taking vibration, and the drawing should say what takes it instead.

This is the single reason a tool controller is not a commodity assembly: the joints that decide the warranty are the ones a placer never touches.

### Coating, and the housing that is not ours

Most tool controllers are coated, because a tool gets rained on and put down in wet grass. It is applied here with connectors and the battery contacts masked.

Two things coating is not: it is not potting, and it is not the housing seal. Potting is not done here, and closing the handle around the board is the tool brand's operation. A design that relies on the coating for water ingress is asking it to do a job it was not specified for — the same argument as on a storage board, at a much lower voltage.

### Batch size, and why the volume argument turns early

A tool programme is usually 1,000 to 5,000 sets, and above roughly 10,000 sets a month a dedicated high-volume line wins on unit price honestly. The reason is not mystery: at that volume the line is set once and run, and changeover stops being a share of the unit cost.

Between those two points, a high-mix floor is the right counterpart, and the thing that decides your price is not the placement count but how many variants you have. A single controller in three firmware variants is one build; three power levels with different bridges is three.

### Where this floor stops

- Motor, gearbox and switch test under load. A dynamometer or torque rig belongs at the tool brand's end-of-line station.
- Potting, overmoulding and closing the housing around the board.
- Tool-level safety or regulatory testing — the certification belongs to the finished tool.
- Volumes above roughly 10,000 sets a month, where a dedicated line wins.

### What to send for a quote

Gerber with copper weights per layer, the stack-up, the BOM with the FETs named by package, the motor tab and terminal drawing with the joint called out, the heatsink interface and torque, the coating and mask list, and the quantity per variant. At 1,000 to 5,000 sets a build is three working days from kitted parts.

The family page is brushless power tool controllers (/applications/power-tool.html). For how the unit price is actually built up, see what is inside a PCBA price (/insights/pcba-cost-per-board.html), and for the inspection argument, what AOI and X-ray can and cannot catch (/insights/what-aoi-xray-cannot-catch.html).

## The rack BMS board spends its life at high voltage and nobody ever looks at it

Source: https://tenmaypcba.com/insights/rack-bms-high-voltage-build-risk.html
Published: 2026-11-19
Summary: The boards in a battery cabinet are judged years after they are built, by something nobody on the assembly floor can run. What that changes about spacing, connectors, contactors and records.

A battery cabinet is the one product family where the board is expected to do nothing for years and then work exactly once, under fault conditions, with somebody's insurance looking at the result. That changes what a buyer should be checking at the assembly stage, and it changes what an assembler can honestly claim. The energy storage family page (/applications/bess.html) carries the process side of that argument; this note is about where the build risk sits.

The three boards in the cabinet are the BMU on each pack, the rack BMS that aggregates them, and the cluster controller that talks to the PCS and the site. The contactor driver and the sensing head that decide whether the cabinet isolates sit on one of those three or on a fourth board of their own.

### What is actually on each board

The BMU measures cell voltages and pack temperature, balances, and reports upward over an isolated bus. It is a small board, repeated sixteen to twenty-four times per rack, and it is the one board where a single assembly defect is multiplied by the count.

The rack BMS aggregates the BMUs, drives the contactors, reads current, and holds the state machine that decides when the cabinet is allowed to close. It carries the isolated sense front end, the contactor driver and the interlock inputs.

The cluster controller is the communication and coordination board — CAN to the PCS, Modbus or Ethernet to the site SCADA, and the logging that somebody will read after an event.

None of these is a difficult board to place. The difficulty is that all three live in a cabinet where the working voltage is hundreds of volts, and every one of them is only as good as the spacing and the connector it was built with.

### Creepage is your certifier's number, not ours

The sense lines that run from a 1000 V stack down to a 5 V ADC need spacing that comes from the standard your pack is certified against — IEC 62619 for industrial storage, UL 1973 in North America — and from your certifier's reading of it. That number belongs on your drawing and in your stack-up.

We build to that drawing, and we will tell you when a spacing looks unbuildable on this floor — 0.30 mm is the finest IC pitch we place, and a coated high-voltage gap is a different constraint from a pitch. What we cannot do is certify the clearance. A certificate on a cabinet is issued against a design, by a body, and an assembler is not that body.

This is the single most common misunderstanding in storage enquiries: the buyer asks whether we can build a board to IEC 62619, and the honest answer is that we can build a board that your certifier will accept, if the drawing already carries their numbers. Asking an assembler to supply the numbers is how a design gets to type test and comes back.

### The connector is where these cabinets actually fail

A rack BMS with twenty BMU drops has a twenty-way harness landing on it. Three things matter more than the board itself:

- Keyed and latched. A sense connector that can be plugged in one position off, or that backs out under vibration, is a fault that appears in year three, not at first power-on.
- Strain relief at the board edge. The harness in a cabinet is heavy and it hangs. A connector held only by its solder joints is a cold joint waiting for a service visit.
- Masking during coating. Coating a connector body instead of masking it is worse than not coating at all: the contact resistance changes and nobody knows.

All three are process decisions that have to be written into the build, not discovered at final inspection.

### THT, contactors and thermal mass

The contactor driver and the pre-charge path are through-hole and heavy copper. Reflow alone does not do this well; it is selective solder or hand solder with the thermal mass managed, and the joints are inspected visually and by pull on the first article.

The reason it matters here rather than on a consumer board is that these joints carry the current that opens the cabinet under fault. A joint that is 80 % filled is a joint that heats. On this floor that work runs in-house — it is one of the reasons a storage board is a comfortable fit rather than a favour.

### Coating: what it does, and what it does not

Conformal coating is standard on storage boards, and it is done here with connectors and test points masked by hand. It buys you condensation and pollution tolerance on a board that sits in a cabinet with a thermal management system that is not perfect.

It does not buy you an IP rating. A coated board in a flooded cabinet is a wet board. If your enclosure design depends on the coating for water ingress, the coating is being asked to do a job it was never specified for.

Potting and encapsulation are the other half of this conversation, and they are not done here. A BMU that has to survive pack-level vibration in a potted module is a different process, and it belongs with the module builder.

### What records we keep, and what they are worth later

Per lot: first-article photographs, SPI results before reflow, AOI results after, X-ray images on the power and QFN joints, and the coating record with the masking set used. Those are filed against the lot and stay retrievable.

Their value is entirely in the year-three question. When a cabinet trips and the investigation reaches the boards, "we built it and here is the X-ray of that joint" is a different conversation from "we have no record".

### Where this floor stops

Say it before the enquiry, not after the type test:

- No high-voltage functional test. We do not have a test bench that takes a rack BMS to working voltage and exercises the contactor sequence. That belongs to the cabinet builder, whose firmware defines pass.
- No pack-level thermal or vibration qualification. The chamber here takes boards, not modules, and it soaks rather than cycles.
- No BMS firmware validation. Balancing behaviour and state-of-charge accuracy are software and cell chemistry questions.
- No IEC 62619 or UL 1973 certification. See above.

### What to send for a quote

The BOM with the DNP and alternate parts marked, the board drawings with your creepage and clearance values on them, the stack-up if you have controlled impedance, the connector list with the mating half named, the coating callout including the mask list, and the quantity.

The scope line on the quote says what is and is not done here. If you need the high-voltage test as part of the order, tell us at enquiry and we will say so plainly rather than at the tooling stage.

For the cabinet-level companion board, the sensing head and trigger driver on the suppression panel, see storage safety boards (/applications/storage-safety.html). The general question of what inspection actually proves is in what AOI and X-ray still cannot catch (/insights/what-aoi-xray-cannot-catch.html), and the test-step decision is in what to do when your assembler has no in-circuit test (/insights/in-circuit-test-outsourcing.html).

## A robot joint board is a circular board built twelve to forty times per machine

Source: https://tenmaypcba.com/insights/robot-joint-many-identical-boards.html
Published: 2026-11-19
Summary: The requirement on a joint board is not difficulty, it is sameness across dozens of units. Where panelisation, test coverage and heat decide whether a robot walks smoothly.

A humanoid or service robot does not have one controller. It has a dozen to forty of the same small board, one per joint, each driving a motor through a gearbox and reading an encoder. The buyer's instinct is to ask whether the board is hard to build. It is not. The real requirement is that board number thirty-seven behaves like board number one, because a robot that walks slightly differently on its left side is a calibration problem that the software team will spend a month on before anyone admits it is a build problem.

That is a different kind of question, and it is one an assembly floor can actually answer.

### Identical is the requirement, not a nice-to-have

Repeatability on this family is produced by four things, none of which is exotic:

- One panel, many boards. Circular joint boards are usually panelised with breakaway tabs or routed with v-cuts. How they are depanelised — and how much stress that puts on the parts nearest the edge — varies by operator unless the method is written down.
- Same paste, same print. A single stencil revision, printed with the same parameters, lot to lot. A print that drifts changes the fillet on the bridge devices and the thermal path under them.
- Same reflow, measured. The profile is developed per board and recorded, so that a reorder six months later starts from a number rather than from memory.
- Same inspection criteria. A board that passes on a Tuesday and would fail on a Friday is not a board; it is an opinion.

At 100 to 1,000 sets, that is 1,200 to 40,000 joint boards. Small enough that the whole run can be one or two panels' worth per build, which makes consistency easier than it sounds — provided nobody re-panels mid-run.

### Density and heat inside a 30 mm circle

A GaN or MOSFET bridge, a gate driver, current sense and an encoder interface in a 30 mm circle with a motor connector on one edge. Three consequences:

- Thermal mass is uneven. The bridge sits on heavy copper and the driver on thin traces. Reflow has to serve both in one pass, and the profile is a compromise that has to be documented.
- Voids under the bridge matter twice over. The joint is the electrical path and the thermal path in a board that has nowhere to put a heatsink.
- Connector landing takes the load. The motor and encoder connectors are the only mechanical interface, and they are what gets yanked during assembly of the joint.

X-ray on the bridge joints is the inspection that matters on this family, and it is worth asking for the images rather than the pass rate.

### What is not done here, and why it matters at prototype speed

A humanoid programme moves quickly, and the temptation is to treat the assembler as a source of everything. It is not:

- Joint calibration, torque-constant measurement and encoder alignment need the actuator and the gearbox. They belong to you.
- Robot-level functional and safety testing and certification of the finished machine are outside this building.
- Volumes above roughly 5,000 joint boards a month are where a dedicated line beats a high-mix floor on unit price. Below that, changeover is a smaller cost than a dedicated line's idle time.

One practical note for a prototype programme: at these volumes, the cost of a revision is close to the cost of the boards. Getting the DFM review right before the stencil is cut is worth more here than on almost any other family, for the simple reason that a mistake is multiplied by the joint count.

### What to send for a quote

Gerber with the panelisation, the stack-up, the BOM with the bridge devices named by package, the centroid, the motor and encoder connector drawing, the inspection callout for the bridge joints, and the quantity in boards and in sets. Also say how the boards will be depanelised if you have a preference, because otherwise it will be decided here.

The family page is robot joint and actuator boards (/applications/humanoid.html). For why a first run and a reorder price differently, see why the second run costs less (/insights/why-the-second-run-costs-less.html), and for the shape of a small-run quote, why fifty pieces cost more per board (/insights/fifty-piece-run-cost.html).

## On a rugged handheld the coating is not a finish, it is the specification

Source: https://tenmaypcba.com/insights/rugged-radio-coating-is-the-product.html
Published: 2026-11-19
Summary: A rugged device survives because of the box and the conformal coat, not the schematic. Where the assembly decision actually lives, and why the shield can dictates the rework path.

A rugged handheld is sold on the environment it survives. Almost none of that survival is electrical. It is the housing, the gasket, the keypad and — on the board — the coating, the shield cans and the connectors that take the abuse. That makes this one of the few families where the assembly step is the product, and where a buyer who treats coating as a cosmetic line item will get a device that passes the drop test once and corrodes on a dock in year two.

Two or three boards typically: a main board, a keypad and display board, and an RF power amplifier board if the design separates it.

### Coating here is a specification, not a finish

Conformal coating is applied here by spray with hand masking. What makes it a specification rather than a finish is that four things have to be written down and then checked:

- What is masked. Connectors, test points, press-fit pins, the antenna contact pads and any pressure-sensitive component. A masked pad that gets a film of acrylic is a contact resistance that drifts in the field, and nobody finds it on the bench.
- What type and thickness. Acrylic, polyurethane and silicone behave differently on thermal cycling and on rework. The callout has to name one and say how it is verified.
- The cure, before the next operation. Coating that is handled before it cures is coating that is scraped off at the next station.
- What happens at rework. A coated board that needs a joint redone gets the coating cut back, the repair made, and the area re-coated — a sequence that has to be agreed or it gets skipped.

The failure this prevents is not dramatic. It is a radio that works for two years in a wet climate and then develops an intermittent that nobody can reproduce in a workshop.

### Shield cans decide the rework path

A rugged device usually carries at least one shield can or a set of fences. The can is either clipped, soldered or a combination, and that choice decides what happens when a board fails at functional test three days into the build.

A soldered can over a section that fails is a board that has to be desoldered, repaired and re-canned, with the shield land taking the thermal cycle twice. A clip-on lid is faster but adds a contact resistance question of its own. Neither is wrong; the mistake is choosing the can for RF reasons at design time and discovering the rework cost at first failure.

This floor solders cans and fences as a standard operation. What it does not do is tell you which can style will cost you less over a product life — that is a decision to make with the RF engineer who knows how often that section is expected to change.

### Press-fit, threads and the parts that get pulled

Rugged devices use press-fit pins and threaded inserts because the buyer expects to open the device. Both are mechanical joints with an electrical job:

- A press-fit pin needs the hole tolerance and the insertion tool specified; a reamed hole gives a joint that passes and later opens.
- A threaded insert in a thin board needs a specified torque, or the insert spins on the second service.

These are drawing decisions. They get executed here, and if the drawing is silent the build uses a house default, which is not the same as a design decision.

### Where this floor stops

- RF alignment, power calibration and waveform conformance. These need a shielded room and the OEM's service software.
- Drop, vibration, IP-rating and salt-fog qualification. These run at an environmental test house against the finished device.
- AS9100, NADCAP processing and ITAR-registered handling for defence programmes. ISO 9001 is what is held, and a programme that requires more should know that before the enquiry, not after.
- Potting, overmoulding and closing the housing. Coating is applied here; the box is not assembled here.

### What to send for a quote

Gerber and stack-up, the BOM, the centroid, the full coating callout including the mask list, the shield-can and press-fit drawing, the connector list with mating halves, and the quantity split across boards. At 100 to 1,000 sets a build is three working days from kitted parts.

The family page is rugged handheld and radio boards (/applications/rugged-radio.html). If you are auditing a new supplier for this kind of work, the five documents that settle an audit (/insights/pcba-supplier-audit-checklist.html) is the companion note, and the coating callout is covered again in what a quote should contain (/insights/pcba-quote-what-it-should-contain.html).

## On AI glasses the hinge is where the yield goes, and it is a board decision

Source: https://tenmaypcba.com/insights/smart-glasses-hinge-yield.html
Published: 2026-11-19
Summary: The electronics are unremarkable; the mechanical path through the hinge is not. What to decide at design time so the flex survives being folded every day for two years.

AI glasses are a small electronics problem inside a hard mechanical one. A main board in the temple, a flex that crosses the hinge to the front, a camera board behind the lens, a 01005-populated layout in a space measured in millimetres. Every one of those is buildable. What kills the product programme is the flex at the hinge, and that is decided on a drawing long before it reaches a line.

### The hinge is a fatigue part with traces in it

The flex crosses a joint that opens and closes every time the glasses are put on. The trace routing there is doing mechanical work: it is being bent, and it will eventually crack. Three design choices decide whether that happens in month three or year three:

- Bend radius, stated and respected. A dynamic bend needs a larger radius than a fold-once flex, and the number belongs on the drawing so that the mechanical and electrical tolerances get resolved before tooling.
- Stiffener placement, and where it stops. A stiffener that ends too close to the bend concentrates stress exactly where you do not want it.
- Trace direction across the bend. Traces perpendicular to the bend line crack; the routing rule exists and gets ignored under space pressure.

On the assembly side, the parts that matter are the connector-to-flex joints at both ends, the underfill decision at those joints, and handling after test — because a flex that is fine at pack-out can be creased by whoever folds it to fit the box.

### Small parts and unforgiving keep-outs

01005 passives, 0.30 mm pitch, and an optical keep-out that must stay flat, clean and uncoated. That combination makes three process steps decisive:

Requirement: What it changes on the line · What it does not
01005 population: Stencil aperture, paste type, placement accuracy, inspection method · Whether the design needed 01005 at all
Optical keep-out: Masking before coating, handling discipline, no-wash chemistry · Lens alignment, which is the optics partner's step
Rigid-flex: Panel support, depanelisation method, connector handling · Hinge life, which is a design margin question

The honest observation about 01005 is that it is a yield cost paid for a space problem. Where the layout allows 0201, 0201 is cheaper and yields better; where it does not, the process has to be built for 01005 rather than borrowed from a 0201 job.

### The commercial truth about this category

Two things are worth saying plainly to anyone building AI glasses:

- Above roughly ten thousand sets a month, this becomes a dedicated-line job. A high-mix floor at 500 to 5,000 sets is the right counterpart below that, and the crossover is real rather than a sales position.
- The test you need is not the test on this floor. Bluetooth, antenna and RF validation, camera tuning, display calibration, acoustic tuning, drop and IP testing — all of it belongs to the product team or a test house. What happens here is assembly and inspection, and being clear about that early is cheaper than discovering it at certification.

### Where this floor stops

- Camera module alignment, image tuning and display calibration. These need the optics and the tuning rig.
- Acoustic tuning, drop testing and IP-rating qualification for the finished frame.
- Potting, overmoulding and final assembly of the temple. Coating is applied here; the frame is not assembled here.
- Any Bluetooth, antenna or RF measurement.

### What to send for a quote

The rigid-flex construction with stiffener and bend callouts, the stack-up, the BOM with the 01005 passives named, the centroid, the connector list, the coating and masking drawing with the optical keep-out marked, and the quantity. At 500 to 5,000 sets the build is three working days from kitted parts; the flex tooling is the long pole.

The family page is AI and AR smart glasses boards (/applications/smart-glasses.html). The package-size trade-off is set out in 01005 vs 0201 (/insights/01005-vs-0201.html), and the process ceilings in what limits 01005 placement yield (/insights/01005-placement-what-limits-yield.html).

## On a telecom line card the impedance comes from the stackup and the shielding from the assembly floor

Source: https://tenmaypcba.com/insights/telecom-impedance-and-shield-cans.html
Published: 2026-11-19
Summary: A line card is a controlled-impedance board with heavy ground copper, shield cans and coax launched at the edge. The two places the assembly step can undo the design.

A telecom line card arrives with the hard problems already solved. The impedance is designed, the stackup is specified, the ground is heavy, the shield fences are drawn. What is left at assembly is execution: build the stackup that was specified, put the cans on without cooking what is underneath, and get the coax and press-fit interfaces landed so they behave.

That is a narrower job than on a power board, and it is more easily spoiled.

### Where assembly can still spoil a controlled stackup

A controlled-impedance design depends on the fabricator holding the stackup, and the assembler cannot change that. What the assembler can change is everything on the surface of it:

- Paste volume on fine-pitch parts near an impedance-critical net. Excessive paste, a spread fillet, or a reflow profile that wicks solder toward a launch all shift local parasitics.
- Rework near an RF launch. A hand-repaired joint beside a coax launch or a filter changes the geometry that was simulated.
- Coating over or under a shielded section, where the callout said to mask it.
- Press-fit insertion force. Too much force bows the board and the launch geometry goes with it; too little gives a joint that passes and later opens.

None of these failures is detectable from the schematic; all of them are detectable from a build record and a first article.

### Shield cans, coax and the order of operations

The order of operations on this family is a genuine engineering decision, not a scheduling preference:

Step: Why the order matters · What goes wrong if it slips
SMT, then X-ray/AOI: Ground pads under cans must be verified before they are covered · A void under a can land is unreachable after assembly
Coax and press-fit: Mechanical operations bend the board · Doing them before final inspection means inspecting a board that will move
Cans and fences: Thermal mass next to sensitive parts · Rework heat near filters shifts their value
Coating, last: Masking costs time and is skipped under pressure · Conductive or absorptive film where the design expects air

A line that has built this family before asks about the can style and the press-fit tooling at quotation. A line that has not asks for the Gerber and nothing else.

### Volume: a few hundred boards is the honest band

Telecom programmes here run 100 to 1,000 sets, and that is deliberate rather than a limitation to apologise for. Carrier-grade volumes in the tens of thousands belong with a dedicated-line EMS, where the test strategy and the automation are built around one product.

What an assembly floor cannot do at this band is substitute for a test house. There is no in-circuit test, no functional test, and no RF alignment or calibration here. Carrier qualification, NEBS or operator approval testing is not performed here either. If your acceptance plan assumes the assembler proves a line card works, the plan is mis-assigned and the fix is cheaper before the purchase order than after.

### What a telecom buyer asks for, and what is on the shelf

The questions that come with this family are consistent: can you hold 0.30 mm pitch, do you X-ray ground pads, do you keep the can and press-fit operation in-house, and what does your first-article pack contain. All four have answers here, and the fourth is the one worth reading carefully — a first-article pack without X-ray images of the ground pads is a pack that skips the part this family cares about.

### Where this floor stops

- Carrier qualification, NEBS or operator approval testing.
- In-house in-circuit or functional test of a line card, including RF alignment and calibration.
- Carrier-grade volumes in the tens of thousands, where a dedicated-line EMS is the right counterpart.
- Enclosure assembly and system-level integration.

### What to send for a quote

Gerber with the stackup and the impedance table, the BOM, the centroid, the can and fence drawing with the ground-pad callout, the press-fit and coax list, the coating and mask drawing, and the quantity. At 100 to 1,000 sets a build is three working days from kitted parts, with the press-fit tooling as the long pole.

The family page is telecom and 5G edge equipment boards (/applications/telecom.html). For the record set that makes this kind of build auditable, what a PCBA quote should contain (/insights/pcba-quote-what-it-should-contain.html), and for what inspection covers, what AOI and X-ray can and cannot catch (/insights/what-aoi-xray-cannot-catch.html).

## A thermal camera core board is a cleaning and masking problem before it is a placement problem

Source: https://tenmaypcba.com/insights/thermal-core-cleaning-and-masking.html
Published: 2026-11-19
Summary: The detector interface is a low-noise analogue board in a small space, and the things that ruin it are flux, dust and a window that should have been masked. Where the build risk sits.

A thermal camera core is two boards — a detector interface and a processing board — plus an optical path that costs more than both. The assembly is not the expensive part. What makes this family awkward is that the failure mode that hurts is invisible on a bench: leakage current and noise from flux residue, contamination on a detector contact, or an unmasked window that got a film of coating on it during a step that was supposed to protect everything else.

Buyers tend to arrive at this page asking about BGA reflow. The BGA is the easy half.

### Why cleanliness outranks placement

The detector interface carries a very small signal from a very expensive sensor. Microamp leakage across a poorly cleaned flux residue, or an ionic contamination path between two fine-pitch pads, shows up not as a dead board but as noise — a slightly worse NETD, a slightly worse image that gets blamed on the detector.

Three process decisions matter more than the placer here:

- Wash or no-wash, and consistently. A no-clean process is fine if the whole build, including rework, is no-clean. The failure is a mixed process where one repair is done with an activated flux and never cleaned.
- Handling between assembly and optics. A board that sits open on a bench collects what the room has in it. This is a small-volume family, 50 to 500 sets, so boards sit around longer than they would in a high-volume line.
- Masking, before coating. The detector contact area, the optical window in a rigid-flex build, and any connector that will be mated in the field.

### Rigid-flex and the mechanical interface

A core that folds into a monocular or a weapon sight usually has a rigid-flex between the detector side and the processing side. That flex is a mechanical part as much as an electrical one: it has to survive being folded once, correctly, and then never again.

What that means for the build:

- The stiffener and the flex bend radius are drawing items. If they are not on the drawing, they get interpreted.
- Connector-to-flex joints take repeated stress in service; the pad design and the soldering method are worth agreeing explicitly rather than leaving to habit.
- The flex is also the thing most likely to be damaged in handling after test, which is why the final pack matters on this family more than most.

### What a build record proves here

Per lot: SPI, AOI, X-ray on the BGA and the detector-side joints, first-article photographs of the masked areas before and after coating, and the wash record if the process is aqueous. Those are the items an optics partner will ask about when an image is soft, because they are the only parts of the chain the board supplier can be held to.

They do not prove the image. Nothing on this floor produces an image.

### Where this floor stops

- Non-uniformity correction, radiometric calibration and NETD measurement. These need a black-body source and the detector vendor's software.
- Image tuning, lens focusing, optical alignment of the core. Optics partner work.
- Airborne, space or defence qualification and export-controlled programme handling. Commercial workmanship only here.
- Potting or full encapsulation. Coating is the only protection applied on this floor.

### What to send for a quote

Gerber with the rigid-flex construction and stiffener callouts, the stack-up including any controlled impedance on the detector side, the BOM with the detector part named and its handling notes, the centroid, the coating and masking drawing, and the quantity. At 50 to 500 sets this is a small-batch build and it is priced as one; the honest reason is in why a fifty-piece run costs more per board (/insights/fifty-piece-run-cost.html).

The family page is thermal and night-vision cores (/applications/thermal-imaging.html). For the inspection argument in general, what AOI and X-ray can and cannot catch (/insights/what-aoi-xray-cannot-catch.html).

---

## On a pressure transmitter the op-amp is the easy part and the seal is not

Source: https://tenmaypcba.com/insights/transmitter-board-seal-not-opamp.html
Published: 2026-11-19
Summary: A round board in an aluminium housing, two wires out, and a drift figure that decides whether the product is believed. Where potting and calibration sit relative to the build.

A pressure transmitter is a small round board inside a sealed aluminium housing on a process pipe, with two wires leaving it. Inside: a ceramic or piezoresistive cell, a low-drift instrumentation amplifier, a 4–20 mA loop stage and a microcontroller. The board is small, the volume is modest, and the product is judged by a number it prints on a certificate.

Assembly's share of that judgement is narrower than buyers expect and more decisive than they assume. Which is why the two failures to sort out before an order are the seal and the drift.

### A small board with an unusually expensive defect

The defect cost on this family is not the board. It is the labour to open a housing on a plant, the downtime of the line it was monitoring, and the credibility of the next shipment. That inverts the usual instinct to optimise unit price:

- Board yield matters less than consistency. A 99 % yield with a drift distribution that moves between lots is worse than 97 % that does not move.
- The analogue chain has to be built the same way every time. Same paste, same profile, same wash, same coat. A single board in a batch that skipped the wash is a service call in a year.
- The housing interface is a drawing item. Board outline, mounting holes and the connector/terminal position determine whether the assembly seals. A board that is 0.2 mm off-centre in a potted cavity is a board that leaks.

### Where the work stops: potting, sealing and calibration

Three steps sit outside this building, and each of them is a place where a programme can quietly fail:

- Potting, encapsulation and any overmoulding of the assembled board. Not done here. A transmitter that depends on a potted cavity is a design that depends on a process this floor does not run, and the partner who does it needs to be in the plan from the first prototype.
- Pressure calibration, the 4–20 mA trim and any accuracy or drift statement. These need a pressure standard; they belong to the sensor maker or a calibration lab.
- Ingress, burst and leak testing of the assembled housing, and the IP rating that comes out of it. Also hazardous-area certification such as ATEX or IECEx, and the documentation behind it.

None of those three is a small omission, and all three are commonly assumed to be included in "PCB assembly".

### What the process controls, and what it only records

It is worth separating two things a supplier will describe in the same sentence:

Controlled here: paste volume, placement, reflow profile, wash or no-wash chemistry, conformal coating with masking, through-hole joint quality on the terminal block, first-article inspection and per-lot records.

Only recorded here: the component date codes and the lot they went into. Which is useful — a drift investigation starts with "which lot" — but is not the same as a measurement.

If a buyer asks "can you guarantee drift under X", the honest answer is no: drift is a design, cell and calibration question. What can be guaranteed is that every board in the lot was built to the same written process, and that the record shows it.

### Two hundred a year is a normal order, and it stays that way

At 100 to 1,000 sets, this is high-mix work, and it stays that way because transmitters are a long-life product with slow model turnover. The practical consequence is that the relationship matters more than the price list: the same boards, built the same way, twice a year, for five years, with a record each time.

### What to send for a quote

Gerber with the board outline and mounting datum, the BOM with the cell and the amp named, the centroid, the terminal block and its torque, the coating and mask drawing, and the quantity with the expected reorder cadence. At 100 to 1,000 sets a build is three working days from kitted parts.

The family page is industrial sensor and transmitter boards (/applications/sensors.html). The potting question in more detail is in potting before test turns a defect into scrap (/insights/parking-sensor-potting-before-test.html), and the record side is in what a PCBA quote should contain (/insights/pcba-quote-what-it-should-contain.html).

---

## A wearable board has almost nothing on it and almost no room for a second attempt

Source: https://tenmaypcba.com/insights/wearable-no-room-for-a-second-attempt.html
Published: 2026-11-19
Summary: The board is tiny, the parts are tiny, and the rework is nearly impossible. What has to be decided before the build, and why volume changes who does the job.

A smart watch or a pair of earbuds carries two or three boards: a main board, a case or charging board, and a sensor carrier. On them: 01005 passives, a 0.30 mm pitch device, a rigid-flex to the display or the button, and an antenna structure that is part of the mechanical design.

Assembling one is not difficult in the way a 400-part server board is difficult. It is difficult because there is no recovery path. A board this small with a part this small is often not reworkable, so the process has to be right the first time rather than inspected and corrected.

### What is actually on the board

Three things set the yield ceiling, and none of them is the placement head:

- Stencil aperture for 01005. A paste deposit that is a little large bridges; a little small leaves an open. The window is narrow and it is a stencil decision, not a machine setting.
- Paste type and reflow. Fine-powder paste and a profile developed for that board. Reusing a profile from a 0402 product is the most common cause of a batch that "should have worked".
- Support and depanelisation. Thin boards, often 0.6 mm or less, with a rigid-flex attached. Flexing during depanel is a cracked joint that passes inspection.

That is why the sensible question to ask an assembler is not "what is your placement accuracy" but "what is your 01005 process, and show me the last board you ran with it".

### Underfill is a design decision, never an assumption

Wearables often need underfill at the rigid-flex joint and around a flip-chip or a fine-pitch package that will see drop energy. Underfill is not a standard step on this floor: it is agreed per design at DFM, because it changes the rework story completely — a board that is underfilled is a board that cannot be repaired, only replaced.

The corollary is worth stating: if your design needs underfill, say so at the enquiry, because that decision affects stencil, handling and inspection, not just one extra operation at the end.

### The tests this family usually needs and will not find here

A wearable has an unusually test-hungry design and an unusually thin test story here. Not available on this floor:

- In-circuit and functional test at volume. There is no ICT and no FCT.
- Bluetooth, antenna or RF validation of the finished device.
- Potting, overmoulding, IP-rating, drop and tumble testing.
- Skin-contact biocompatibility, and battery-pack certification such as UN 38.3 or IEC 62133.

What is available: assembly, SPI, AOI, X-ray where the design calls for it, coating with masking, and a lot record. For a programme whose acceptance criteria lean on functional test, that gap has to be closed with a fixture you own — the arrangement in what to do when your assembler has no in-circuit test (/insights/in-circuit-test-outsourcing.html).

### Where volume turns this family into somebody else's job

At 500 to 5,000 sets, a high-mix floor is the right counterpart and the price is mostly process and inspection. In the tens of thousands, the equation flips: the cost is no longer placement, it is test coverage and handling automation, and a consumer-electronics EMS with a dedicated line will beat a high-mix floor honestly rather than by cutting corners.

Knowing that crossover in advance is what stops a programme from being moved mid-qualification, which is the most expensive way to learn it.

### What to send for a quote

Gerber with the stack-up and the rigid-flex construction, the BOM with the 01005 parts and the fine-pitch device named, the centroid, the underfill and coating callouts with the mask list, the depanelisation method if you have one, and the quantity. At 500 to 5,000 sets a build is three working days from kitted parts.

The family page is wearables and hearables boards (/applications/wearables.html). For the package decision, 01005 vs 0201 (/insights/01005-vs-0201.html); for the process ceilings, what limits 01005 placement yield (/insights/01005-placement-what-limits-yield.html); and for the hinge-and-flex version of the same problem, AI glasses and the hinge (/insights/smart-glasses-hinge-yield.html).

## PCBA since 2008: what a founding date proves, and what it does not

Source: https://tenmaypcba.com/insights/pcba-since-2008.html
Published: 2026-11-18
Summary: The date proves the legal entity persisted. It says nothing about whether the SMT floor existed then. Three checks separate an old company from a long-running assembly operation — and one of them is asking for a record from a year you choose.

"PCBA since 2008" is on a thousand supplier profiles and it is almost never checked. That is odd, because it is the cheapest question in sourcing to verify and the one with the most direct bearing on whether a quote will still mean something in two years.

This note is about the check, not about us. It ends with our own answer, stated plainly, including the part of our history that gets misread.

### The date is a field on a document, and you can ask for the document

Every legally registered Chinese company has a business licence (营业执照) carrying four things a buyer can use: the registered name, the unified social credit code, the date of establishment, and the registered address. The date of establishment is not a marketing claim. It is printed by the registry.

So the first move is not to read an About page. It is to ask for the licence, then compare it against everything else the supplier has told you:

- Does the registered name match the certificate holder name, the bank beneficiary, and the quotation header?
- Does the registered address match the factory address you were given?
- Does the date of establishment match the "since" claim on the website and on third-party profiles?

Three mismatches out of three is a trading office. One or two is a conversation. This is the same document set the supplier audit checklist (/insights/pcba-supplier-audit-checklist.html) is built around, and the date is the field people skip because it feels like trivia.

### What the date does not prove

Here is the part suppliers would rather you did not think about: an old company can be a young assembler. The two facts live in different places and there is no registry that records when a particular SMT line was installed.

Three ways the two diverge, all common:

- The entity is older than the plant. A trading company or a design house that existed for years, then added assembly capacity later. The licence date is honest and the assembly experience is five years old.
- The owners restarted under a new entity. The old company closed, the same people registered a new one, the website kept the original "since" year. You will find the year on the site and a recent establishment date on the licence.
- The company changed product, correctly and openly. A business that genuinely did something else first and moved into assembly. Nothing dishonest — but the years spent on the earlier product are not years of assembly experience, and a buyer counting them is counting the wrong thing.

Our own case is the third one, and it is worth spelling out because an old profile of ours still causes exactly this misreading (see below).

### The check that actually separates them

Search history is weak evidence. Dated internal records are strong, because they are expensive to fake and cheap to sample.

Ask for a record from a year you choose. Not "your oldest first-article report" — that lets the supplier pick the best-looking document. Name a year — 2016, 2011 — and ask for a first-article report, a job traveller, or an inspection record from that year for a board of that type. Four outcomes:

What comes back: What it means
A dated record matching the year you named: Strong. Someone kept an archive, and the archive reaches back.
A record from a different year, offered with an explanation: Fair. Ask why the year you named is missing before deciding.
Only certificates and photos: Weak. Photos carry no date that can be checked.
A promise to look and no follow-up: The answer is in the silence.

Three more that cost one email each:

- Customer references with dates attached, not logos. "They have supplied us since 2019, here is the part number" is checkable by asking the reference. A wall of logos is not.
- Equipment nameplates. Every placer and reflow oven has a manufacturer plate with a serial. A 2023 machine on a floor that claims 2009 is not a scandal — lines get replaced — but the mix of ages tells you whether the floor has been running continuously or was built in one go.
- The certificate, as issued rather than cropped. The certificate number, the scope statement and the holder name are what a buyer checks against the issuing body. A cropped image is not a document.

### Our own case: the LED line, in the right order

Tenmay was founded on 2008-01-09 as a contract electronics assembly business. That has been the business continuously since.

At one point the company developed its own LED lighting product line and sold it under the ledsztm.com brand. It was a product the company made, sitting on top of the assembly business — not a change in what the company was. The line was later closed so the company could concentrate on assembly.

The sequence is assembly, then an LED product line, then assembly only. It is not a move from lighting into electronics.

This matters practically, because the misreading is easy to arrive at honestly. An old profile of ours on a B2B directory still lists the main category as lighting and still says the company has five years of experience — a sentence written more than a decade ago and never updated. A buyer who finds that page first, and reads it as the company's origin, will conclude the PCBA business is a reinvention. It is not. But you should not resolve that by taking our word for it, which is the whole point of the previous section: name a year and ask for a record from it.

What is still true today: LED driver boards are assembled here, as boards, for customers who build lighting products. Building a fixture and building the board inside it are different jobs, and we do the second one.

### What we claim, and what we do not

The useful half of a capability statement is the negative half.

Held: ISO 9001:2015, certified under GB/T 19001-2016, certificate 38822Q00487R0S. Note the edition: the certificate is issued against the 2015 edition, which ISO withdrew on 2026-09-16 in favour of ISO 9001:2026. Transition status sits with the certification body, and we say so rather than implying the current edition.

Not held: IATF 16949, ISO 13485, certified IPC Class 3 process, AS9100, AS9102 first-article reporting, NADCAP special processes, ITAR registration. Bare PCB fabrication is not done here — boards are bought from qualified partner fabs, and this is an assembly house. A programme that requires any of those is a programme we should decline early rather than quote and disappoint.

Running today: eight SMT lines, 5,000,000 placement points per day, from 01005 upward; through-hole and hand soldering; SPI, AOI and X-ray in line; conformal coating; device programming; minimum order 50 pieces, three working days standard once the kit is complete.

### One hour, in this order

- Ask for the business licence. Check establishment date, credit code, registered address, registered name against the quotation header.
- Ask for the ISO 9001 certificate as issued. Check the holder name against the licence and the scope against what you are buying.
- Name a year and ask for a first-article report from it.
- Ask one customer reference for a date and a part number.
- Ask what the supplier does not hold. A supplier with a written negative list has thought about which programmes it should refuse.

None of that requires a flight, and it is the difference between buying years and buying a story. The date is worth exactly what your ability to check it is worth — so ask it of every supplier in the comparison, not just the one you already like.

## Who owns the optics on a dashcam build?

Source: https://tenmaypcba.com/insights/dashcam-optics-not-an-assembly-step.html
Published: 2026-11-17
Summary: Lens alignment is not an assembly step. A build that treats the sensor board as the product will pass inspection and still miss focus in the field.

A dashcam is three boards — a sensor carrier, a mainboard, and a display board — inside a housing that clips to a windscreen and gets hot in summer. Two of those boards are ordinary dense SMT work. The third carries an image sensor and a lens, and that is where the sourcing boundary usually gets drawn in the wrong place.

### The sensor board is the product

Everything the customer judges — sharpness, colour, low-light performance, whether the plate is readable at speed — comes from the sensor and the optics, not from the SoC. The mainboard processes what the sensor delivers. If the sensor module is compromised, no amount of processing recovers it.

That has a sourcing consequence: the sensor carrier is the one board where "we assembled it and it passed inspection" is not an answer. A board can be perfectly assembled and still produce a soft image, because the lens was focused against a target that does not match the real scene, or because the holder was seated with a tilt that only appears after the housing is clipped shut.

### What is and is not an assembly step

Step: Whose process · Can an assembler do it?
Place and reflow the sensor carrier: Assembler · Yes — fine pitch, 01005 passives, 0.3 mm pitch
X-ray the SoC and memory joints: Assembler · Yes — hidden joints under the package
Mount the lens holder: Depends on the design · Only if the drawing specifies the adhesive and cure
Active alignment and focus: Optics house · No — needs a target, a chart and a lens fixture
Final image validation: Brand or optics house · No — needs the firmware and the acceptance criteria
Environmental and thermal soak: Brand · No — that is a product-level test

The middle two rows are the boundary. Active lens alignment is not an assembly step; it is a metrology step that requires a collimator, a test chart and a decision about what "in focus" means for the product. An assembly house that says it will "fit the lens" and does not have that equipment is doing passive placement and calling it alignment.

### The X-ray is the assembly-side control that matters

On the mainboard, the SoC and the memory are the risk. Both sit under packages where a void or an incomplete joint is invisible from the surface, and both are the components whose failure presents as an intermittent camera rather than a dead one.

X-ray on those joints is the control that an assembler genuinely owns. Ask for it explicitly, and ask whether it is every board or a sample — the answer changes the price and the assurance.

The sensor carrier has its own version of the same problem: the sensor's own pads are fine pitch and the flex attach is a mechanical joint that gets pulled when the housing is assembled. A lifted flex trace passes inspection and fails when the unit is clipped to a windscreen.

### The thermal decision belongs to the housing, not the board

A dashcam sits in direct sun behind glass. The housing design and the thermal path decide whether the SoC throttles; the board's job is to conduct heat out of the package through thermal vias and pad geometry.

Where this becomes a sourcing question is in the specification: if the thermal pad and via pattern were designed for a metal housing and you switch to plastic, the assembler cannot fix it. Worth raising at DFM rather than at the third batch.

### When to split the sensor from the rest

Split when you have an optics partner who already does alignment and validation, because they own the acceptance criteria and you want one party answering for image quality. Keep the boards together when the volumes are small and the sensor is a standard module with a factory-focused lens — no alignment step, no split needed.

The rule is simple: split where the acceptance criteria live, not where the boards are.

### What to put in the enquiry

- Gerber, BOM and centroid for all three boards, plus the stack-up for the sensor carrier.
- Whether the lens is pre-focused or aligned in your process. If it is aligned, say who does it and what target is used.
- The X-ray requirement, stated per board: SoC, memory, or both, sample or full.
- The housing material and the thermal path, at DFM stage rather than after the first batch.
- The batch band. This family normally runs 500 sets to 5,000 sets; below that, the fixture and first-article work for a fine-pitch sensor carrier dominates.

The dashcam board page (/applications/dashcam.html) says plainly that active lens alignment is not an assembly step here, which is the boundary worth testing any supplier against. The robot vacuum mainboard (/applications/robot-vacuum.html) carries the same density and the same under-package risk, and the parking sensor board (/applications/parking-sensor.html) is the other family where a small board is dominated by what happens after assembly. What AOI and X-ray cannot catch (/insights/what-aoi-xray-cannot-catch.html) explains the inspection gap this family lives with.

A sharp image on the bench and a sharp image at 100 km/h are different tests. Decide who runs the second one before you place the order.
