## Sharing a build stack between servo drives and VFDs

Source: https://tenmaypcba.com/insights/servo-drive-shared-stack-with-vfd.html
Published: 2026-11-17
Summary: One stack, two products, smaller batches. The saving is real; the risk is that a design nobody else can build becomes a supplier with pricing power.

A servo drive and a variable frequency drive are not the same product sold twice. A VFD holds a motor at a speed; a servo holds a motor at a position, and does it thousands of times a second. What they share is a power stage, a gate drive, an isolation barrier and a set of through-hole terminals carrying real current. In sourcing terms, they share a build stack.

### What is genuinely shared

Element: VFD · Servo · Shared?
Power stage: IGBT bridge, DC bus, electrolytics · Often IGBT or MOSFET bridge, DC bus · Yes — same solder and thermal problem
Gate drive: Isolated, one per phase · Isolated, faster switching · Yes in structure, not in tuning
Encoder interface: Usually none, or a simple pulse input · Differential pairs, high-rate, noise-critical · No — servo only
Control: Speed loop · Position and velocity loop · Same silicon, different firmware
Terminals: Mains, motor, braking · Mains, motor, encoder, STO · Yes, and both are through-hole

Two of the four boards in a typical servo — the power board and the control board with the encoder front end — land in the same process window as a VFD. That is why the families are usually built by the same kind of shop: heavy copper, thermal mass, through-hole terminals, conformal coating, batches measured in tens to hundreds of sets rather than thousands.

### The saving from one stack

Consolidating at one assembler buys three concrete things:

- One reflow profile development. A power board with a thick copper pour and a row of electrolytics heats unevenly; the profile is developed per board, not inherited. If the servo power board is a variant of the VFD power board, part of that work carries over.
- One coating specification and one mask drawing. Both families are usually conformally coated. One supplier, one coating material, one set of keep-clear zones.
- One conformance conversation. If both product lines sit under the same quality system and the same documentation, an audit covers both.

At 50 sets to 500 sets per build, those three items are not a rounding error. They are frequently the difference between a quote that works and one that does not.

### Where the consolidation turns against you

The risk is not commercial, it is structural. If one assembler holds the stencil, the programme, the profile, the coating mask and the first-article history for both product lines, then moving the build means re-creating all of it somewhere else. That is a real barrier, and a supplier who understands it may price accordingly.

Three symptoms worth watching for:

- The quote stops moving. When a re-quote on a mature design comes back flat for two years while material moves, the setup has probably become rent.
- The second source cannot be qualified in time. Qualify a second assembler on the simpler of the two boards while volumes are low. It is much easier than doing it during a capacity crisis.
- Documentation lives only at the supplier. The stencil files, the profile and the mask drawing are your product's manufacturing definition. Ask for copies at every revision.

### The encoder front end is the servo-specific decision

Everything else in a servo drive is a VFD problem with tighter timing. The encoder interface is not. Differential pairs at high rate, a shield that has to be terminated at one end and not the other, and a connector that must survive a cable being pulled — that is a four-layer fine-pitch board with a specific routing requirement, and it is where a servo build fails first.

Practical consequences for the enquiry: ask for the encoder board's differential pair routing rules and the stack-up, not just the Gerber. If an assembler treats it as a digital board and routes it like one, the drive will run and then lose position under noise. That failure appears in the field, not on the bench, and it is expensive to attribute.

### When to split

- Different batch bands. If the servo runs at tens of sets and the VFD at hundreds, the changeover economics diverge and the split becomes natural.
- Different customer segments with different audit needs. A machine-tool buyer and a pump buyer do not ask for the same records.
- You need a second source for supply security, and it will only take one of the two products.

### What to put in the enquiry

- Gerber, BOM, centroid and the stack-up for each board.
- Whether the servo power board is a variant of an existing design — if it is, say what changed, because the profile development may be partially reusable.
- Coating type and keep-clear zones, and whether the encoder connector is coated.
- The differential pair specification for the encoder interface.
- Both batch bands, stated separately. This family normally runs 50 to 500 sets; a quote that assumes 500 will look wrong at 50.

The servo drive page (/applications/servo.html) states the shared stack with the VFD family and the 50 to 500 set band. The VFD page (/applications/vfd.html) covers the three-board set and the through-hole work, and the HMI and PLC I/O family (/applications/hmi.html) has the same isolation-discipline problem in a colder thermal environment. For the commercial side of small batches, why a fifty-piece run costs more per board (/insights/fifty-piece-run-cost.html) is the arithmetic.

Two products on one stack is a good position. The mistake is discovering, three years in, that it is a good position for one party only.

On an unchanged revision the standard build here is 3 days from kitted parts, which is the number to plan a reorder against rather than a promise about component lead time.

Last reviewed: 2026-11-17 · Review a drive board stack: WhatsApp (https://wa.me/8617361058693)

## Finding a real PCBA factory in Shenzhen, when half of them are trading offices

Source: https://tenmaypcba.com/insights/shenzhen-pcba-factory-guide.html
Published: 2026-11-17
Summary: A trading company is not automatically a problem. Quoting as a factory when you are not one is. Three checks separate the two, and none of them needs a flight.

Shenzhen assembles a large share of the world's electronics, and a meaningful share of the companies presenting themselves as factories are trading offices with a shop floor they visit. Three checks settle it in under an hour: does the ISO certificate name match the company you are paying, can they state a process limit as a number, and will they show you the line on a live call without a day's notice.

### Why the trading company exists at all

It is worth saying first: a trading company is not automatically a problem. A good one consolidates suppliers, handles documentation and saves you a factory relationship you do not have the volume for. Plenty of buyers are better served by one.

The problem is not knowing which one you are talking to, because the two carry different risks:

: Real factory · Trading office
Process changes: Decided on their floor; you can see the limit · Negotiated with a third party you never meet
Quality escapes: Traceable to a lot record they own · Traceable to a supplier who may deny it
Price movement: Component and rate mechanics visible · Margin absorbs the movement, opacity increases
Capacity claim: "8 lines, of which 2 are free next week" · "We have partner factories"

Neither column is dishonest by itself. The failure mode is a trading office quoting as a factory: you buy on the assumption of control that does not exist.

### Check 1 — Certificate name vs company you pay

This is the fastest test and the one most often skipped.

Take the ISO certificate and the proforma invoice, and read the holder name and the beneficiary name side by side. Same name, same entity — good. Different names, ask why in writing, before payment.

Legitimate reasons exist: a Hong Kong collection entity, a group structure, a name romanised differently on the certificate. We are an example of the last one: our certificate is issued to Shenzhen Tengmei Technology Co., Ltd., our registered name is 深圳腾镁科技有限公司, and our English trading name is Shenzhen Tenmay Technology Co., Ltd. The unified social credit code 91440300670000384N is what links all three — and we publish the mapping so nobody has to take it on faith.

The illegitimate version is a beneficiary that appears at the last minute, is offshore, or is a personal account. That is where deposits disappear.

### Check 2 — Can they state a process limit as a number?

Ask three questions and listen for numbers:

- "What is your finest IC pitch?" → 0.30 mm is an answer; "fine pitch capable" is not.
- "What is the largest board you place?" → 800 × 480 mm is an answer.
- "What is your daily placement capacity?" → 5,000,000 points per day across eight lines is an answer, and it is checkable against the machine count.

A trading office can repeat marketing numbers. What a trading office cannot do is assign the work to a line, a machine and a shift. So follow up: "Which line would this board run on, and what else is booked on it that week?" The answer either refers to their own schedule or it does not.

### Check 3 — The unannounced live call

Not a video they sent you. A call you schedule, where you choose the targets while the camera is walking.

Ask to see:

- The X-ray station, with someone reading an image on screen
- The SPI screen showing the job currently on the line
- The feeder cart for a live job, with a reel barcode visible
- A lot record for the batch on the floor, opened in front of you
- The coating booth, with masking prepared for a real board

None of these can be improvised in five minutes in an office. All of them can be shown in a factory that is actually running.

### What Shenzhen does not give you

Say the limits out loud, because geography is not a capability:

- Certification is not implied by location. Shenzhen has plants at every level, from one manual bench to fully automated. The address tells you nothing about the certificate.
- Not every board should be built here. If your programme needs IATF 16949 inside a vehicle chain, ISO 13485 for a medical device, or in-circuit test under the assembly roof, choose a plant that holds those — including if that plant is not us.
- Cheap quotes at high volume are a different business. Above a few thousand pieces a month, a larger plant's hourly rate usually beats a small-batch specialist. That is arithmetic, not loyalty.

### What we publish, so you can check it against the list above

Check: Our published answer
Legal identity: 深圳腾镁科技有限公司 · USCC 91440300670000384N · trading as TENMAY
Certificate: ISO 9001, 38822Q00487R0S, holder name Shenzhen Tengmei Technology Co., Ltd.
Finest pitch: 0.30 mm · finest passive 01005 (0.4 × 0.2 mm)
Largest board: 800 × 480 mm, double-sided
Capacity: 8 × Yamaha YSM20/YSM10, 5,000,000 points per day
Minimum order: 50 pcs, same for turnkey, partial turnkey and consigned kit
Lead time: 3 working days from kitted parts
Not held: IATF 16949 · ISO 13485 · third-party IPC Class 3 · in-house ICT/FCT · bare-board fabrication
Live audit: Available on request, unscripted, targets chosen by you

If any line here does not match what you see on a call, treat that as the most important data point in the whole exercise.

The document checks in this note are compressed into a checklist on the supplier audit page (/insights/pcba-supplier-audit-checklist.html); the camera checks are expanded on a remote audit that proves something (/insights/virtual-factory-audit.html). The entity record itself sits on company.html (/company.html).

## The 800 mm board is not the hard part of a treadmill build

Source: https://tenmaypcba.com/insights/treadmill-large-board-mechanics.html
Published: 2026-11-17
Summary: Buyers worry about board size and get caught by a console harness and a motor drive in a sealed plastic housing. Here is where to spend the attention instead.

A treadmill is two boards — a motor drive board in the base and a console board on the handlebar — plus a harness that runs the length of the machine through a frame that flexes under a running load. Buyers arriving at this family usually ask about board size first. Size is the easy part.

### What the size limit actually constrains

The motor drive board can run to the largest panel this floor handles, which is a real capability boundary: it decides which line the job can be assigned to and whether it fits at all. That is worth confirming before anything else, because a design that does not fit has no other question.

But once it fits, board size stops being the risk. A large power board is heavy copper and thermal mass; the profile is developed per board rather than inherited, and that is a one-time engineering task with a known cost.

### Where the failures actually are

Failure: Where it starts · Detectable at the assembler?
Console goes dead or flickers: Ribbon harness or connector lift after the handlebar is tightened · Partly — a pull test on the connector, not AOI
Motor drive overheats: Thermal path in a sealed plastic housing; electrolytic life · No — housing-level design, not board
Speed reads wrong under load: Current sense path contamination or a marginal shunt joint · Partly — visible joints yes, drift no
Incline or speed drifts: Connector contact resistance after vibration · No — appears in service
Board works, safety key fails: Key switch is a harness and enclosure item · No — not a board function

The pattern is consistent: the failures that generate service calls are mechanical and thermal, and the ones your inspection can see are the ones that rarely fail. That is worth knowing before you spend the quality budget in the wrong place.

### The connector is the product

On this family a connector that lifts when the console is bolted down reads as an intermittent fault that no AOI will ever find, and it will be attributed to the board. Two process items reduce that:

- A stated insertion and pull requirement on the console connector, checked at first article.
- Strain relief designed in, not added as a note. If the harness hangs off the connector with nothing taking the load, the joint takes it instead.

Most treadmill boards that come back from the field are not badly soldered. They are mechanically over-stressed at one connector, and the solder did what it was told.

### Thermal, inside a closed plastic base

The drive board sits in a base with limited airflow, and the electrolytics on it have a life that is a function of temperature. The board's contribution is thermal vias and copper area under the switching devices; the housing's contribution is whether the heat has anywhere to go.

This is a DFM conversation, not an assembly fix. If the design was thermally signed off on a bench in free air, the first summer is the real test. Worth raising at DFM: what the maximum expected ambient in the base is, and whether the capacitor choice assumed it.

### The two boards are built in different worlds

The motor drive is a power board: heavy copper, through-hole terminals, thermal vias, conformal coating because the base sees sweat and dust. The console is a light board with a display, buttons and a long harness, versioned for cosmetics.

They also move at different speeds, like the e-bike pair: the console changes when the brand wants a new look, the drive changes when the motor or the deck does. Quoting them on separate lines is what keeps a console restyle from reopening the drive approval — and at 200 sets to 2,000 sets, sharing one setup across both is worth asking about if they ship together anyway.

### What to put in the enquiry

- Gerber, BOM and centroid for both boards, plus board dimensions stated explicitly so the panel fit can be confirmed.
- The maximum board dimension if the drive board is near the size limit — this decides line assignment.
- Coating requirement and keep-clear zones, including the terminal blocks.
- The console connector specification: part number, insertion force, and how it is strain-relieved.
- Expected ambient in the base, so the thermal question gets answered at DFM.
- Whether both boards ship on one purchase order, since that changes setup allocation.

The treadmill and fitness control board page (/applications/treadmill.html) states the two-board split, the largest panel size carried and the batch band. The VFD family (/applications/vfd.html) is the closest process relative — heavy copper beside a fine-pitch control board — and the e-bike controller (/applications/ebike.html) repeats the pattern of a power board and a cosmetic board on one shipment. Why a fifty-piece run costs more per board (/insights/fifty-piece-run-cost.html) explains the setup arithmetic that decides whether sharing one setup is worth it.

Confirm the board fits, then spend the rest of the attention on the harness and the heat. Those are what come back.

Last reviewed: 2026-11-17 · Send a board pair for review: WhatsApp (https://wa.me/8617361058693)

## Quoting a VFD as three boards or as one set

Source: https://tenmaypcba.com/insights/vfd-three-boards-one-quote.html
Published: 2026-11-17
Summary: Line-by-line tells you where the money is; set pricing tells you what a drive actually costs to build. Ask for both, then decide which number you are managing.

A variable frequency drive is three boards with three different process profiles: a control board with isolated gate drive, an IGBT power board carrying the DC bus and current sensors, and a keypad board. A drive missing one board is not shippable. That single fact drives the whole quoting decision.

### Two ways to price the same build

Approach: What it answers · Where it misleads
Three separate lines: Where the cost sits: which board carries the through-hole work, which carries the coating, which is trivial · You cannot tell what a shippable drive costs
One set price: What a drive costs to build and ship · It hides an expensive board inside a blended number
Both, with the set as the commercial unit: Everything above · Nothing much — it just takes more paper

Buyers usually ask for one or the other. The useful enquiry asks for both, because they support different decisions: the line breakdown is what you need to redesign cost out, and the set price is what you need to plan a purchase order.

### Why the set is the real unit

The keypad board is small and cheap until it is not. Membrane tails, a segment or dot-matrix driver and one harness connector: low value, high nuisance. A wrong footprint there turns into a hand-reworked batch and the drive still cannot ship.

Compare that with the power board, which may run up to the largest panel this floor handles and carries the IGBT stage, the DC-bus electrolytics and the current sensors. It is heavy copper, large thermal mass, through-hole terminals and bus bars that must be soldered without cooking the devices beside them.

Three boards, three very different cost drivers, one shipment. If a supplier quotes you a keypad price and a power board price but cannot state a set price, they have not priced the thing you are buying.

### The reorder question is where set pricing pays

On drives, the demand shape is not consumer growth. It is spare-board and maintenance orders arriving in tens and hundreds rather than thousands, and a build measured in days rather than weeks. The buyer's real question is "how fast can I restock a drive", not "what is the cheapest board".

Which is why the first-order quote and the reorder quote should be separated in the paperwork. The band here is 50 sets to 500 sets. The first order pays for stencil, programme, profile development and first-article approval. The reorder, on an unchanged revision, does not. A supplier who keeps the programme and the approval on file can quote a reorder against that same revision, and the number drops for a reason that is visible rather than negotiated.

### What the through-hole content does to the price

Drives carry terminal blocks, relays and bus connections that have to be hand or selectively soldered. A pure placement house subcontracts exactly this step, which is why drives are a comfortable fit for a floor that runs it in-house and a poor fit for one that does not.

Two questions expose this quickly:

- Is the through-hole work done in-house, or subcontracted? If subcontracted, the schedule has a second party in it.
- Is conformal coating done in-house? Drives usually specify it; masking connectors and test points by hand is real labour, not a rounding error.

### What inspection proves here, and what it does not

SPI runs before reflow on the fine-pitch side, AOI after reflow, and X-ray on the IGBT and thermal-pad joints where voiding under a power device is invisible from the surface and presents later as a hot drive.

What none of it proves is that the drive works. In-circuit and functional test with a load bank are not assembly operations — the pass criteria belong to the firmware and the motor. If your process requires full functional test at the assembler, that is a different supplier category, and saying so early saves both sides a month.

### What to put in the enquiry

- Gerber, BOM and centroid for all three boards, plus the stack-up for the power board.
- Which board runs to the largest panel size, so the line assignment can be confirmed against the size limit.
- The coating requirement and which connectors and test points must stay clear.
- First-order and reorder quantities separately, since they are priced differently and honestly so.
- Whether a set price is available, in addition to the three lines.
- Whether functional test is expected at the assembler. Ask it explicitly; do not let it be discovered at handover.

The VFD and inverter page (/applications/vfd.html) states the three-board split, the batch band and the standard build time from kitted parts. The servo drive family (/applications/servo.html) shares the power stage and adds an encoder front end, and the treadmill control board (/applications/treadmill.html) is the other family where the largest board size is the deciding capability. Why a fifty-piece run costs more per board (/insights/fifty-piece-run-cost.html) is the arithmetic behind the first-order versus reorder gap.

Ask for the set price. Then ask what the second order costs. The two numbers together tell you more about a supplier than either one alone.

On an unchanged revision the standard build here is 3 days from kitted parts, which is the number to plan a reorder against rather than a promise about component lead time.

## A remote factory audit that actually proves something

Source: https://tenmaypcba.com/insights/virtual-factory-audit.html
Published: 2026-11-17
Summary: A prepared video tour cannot prove the lot on the line is yours. An unscripted live call can prove the equipment, the people and the records are real — which is most of what a site visit buys you.

A remote audit works if it is unscripted: you schedule the call, you name the stations while the camera is walking, and nobody gets a day's notice about the route. What a prepared video tour cannot prove is that the lot on the line is yours — so ask for the job traveller and the first-article photo to be shown on camera, with the revision visible.

### What a live call can prove, and what it cannot

Can prove:

- The equipment exists, is powered, and matches the capability claim (machine model readable on the frame)
- People are where the process says they should be, and they are doing the work described
- Materials, reels and boards are physically present in the stated condition
- A record can be produced and opened live, rather than described

Cannot prove:

- That the lot on the line is your lot
- That the process on that particular shift is the process on every shift
- That the yield figure someone quotes you is real
- That the plant will still be running your programme in eighteen months

Be honest with yourself about the boundary: a remote audit reduces risk, it does not certify a supplier. It is far better than nothing and considerably weaker than standing on the floor.

### The five things to ask the camera to show

Choose them while on the call. In this order, because each one depends on the previous being real:

#: Ask for · What a fake looks like
1: Walk to the X-ray station — is someone reading an image on screen? · A machine visible, no operator, no screen lit, or a still image
2: The SPI screen with the job currently on the line · A generic dashboard, or "we can't show that"
3: The feeder cart for a live job, with a reel barcode visible · Reels present but no link to a program or a revision
4: The lot record for the batch on the floor, opened live · A template, a blank form, or a photo of a printed sheet
5: The coating booth, with masking prepared for a real board · A booth, no work in progress, no masking fixtures

The pattern to watch for is not "no". It is "that station is not running today" repeated five times. Any single station can legitimately be idle. All five cannot.

### Records to have emailed during the call

Ask for these to be sent while you are still on the line — it tests responsiveness and keeps the audit from turning into a promise:

- First-article report for a lot comparable to yours, with the revision it was built against
- AOI or X-ray images from that lot, filed against the lot number
- Incoming bare-board inspection record — thickness, warpage, finish, panel markings
- Component incoming check — part number, quantity, date code, packaging integrity
- Certificate of conformance as issued with a shipment

If the answer is "we will send it after the call", note how many days it takes. That turnaround is a preview of how the programme will run.

### Red flags on a prepared tour

- A route that never leaves one aisle. Eight lines cannot all be visible from one walkway.
- Nobody working at the machine being shown. Ask why, and listen for whether the answer names a real production condition.
- A supervisor who answers every technical question and no operator who speaks. The line knows things the office does not.
- Reels with no labels, or labels facing away. Reel-to-program binding is a real control; a tour that avoids it is avoiding the question.
- Reluctance about the X-ray screen specifically. X-ray is where voiding and head-in-pillow are read. It is also where a plant without a real inspection habit gets exposed.
- "Our engineer is not available." Then reschedule with the engineer. Do not proceed on a sales call.

### What to do after the call

Three things, same day, while it is fresh:

- Write down what you saw as facts and what you inferred separately. The gap between them is your residual risk.
- Send a short list of follow-up questions — the ones the call raised. Speed and specificity of the reply is a second data point about the supplier.
- Ask for one photo of a finished lot, packing stage, with the label visible. It is a cheap test of whether photos actually get taken on that floor.

### How we run this

You pick the targets, we walk. No route is sent in advance and no station is pre-lit for the call. Typical things buyers ask for here: the X-ray screen with a BGA on it, the SPI result for the job running, the feeder cart with the reel barcode, the coating booth with masking in place, and the lot record for the batch on the floor.

Also on camera if you ask: a first-article photo from a past lot, the incoming bare-board check, and the machine program bound to a revision.

What we will say on the call, before you ask: in-circuit and functional test are not in the building, bare boards are bought rather than fabricated, and IATF 16949 / ISO 13485 / third-party IPC Class 3 are not held. If any of those is a requirement for your programme, the call has still been worth it — you found out in twenty minutes instead of at tooling.

The document half of the audit is on the supplier audit checklist (/insights/pcba-supplier-audit-checklist.html); the question of whether the supplier is a factory at all is on finding a real PCBA factory in Shenzhen (/insights/shenzhen-pcba-factory-guide.html). The "not held" list we read out on these calls is published on company.html (/company.html).

## What is PCBA? PCB vs PCBA, and what the extra letter buys you

Source: https://tenmaypcba.com/insights/what-is-pcba.html
Published: 2026-11-17
Summary: PCB is copper, mask and silkscreen with no parts. PCBA is the board plus components, soldered and inspected. The distinction decides who can quote you and which half of the job you are buying.

PCBA means printed circuit board assembly: a bare PCB with the components soldered onto it, inspected, and ready to install. PCB is the bare board on its own — copper, mask and silkscreen with no parts. A PCBA supplier therefore buys or is given bare boards and adds the assembly step, which is exactly the split we work in: bare boards from partner fabs, everything after that in our Shenzhen plant.

### The three-letter difference, stated plainly

Term: What it is · Who makes it
PCB: The bare board: substrate, copper traces, solder mask, surface finish. No components. · A PCB fabricator (a "board house")
PCBA: That board plus components, soldered and inspected. A functional assembly. · A PCBA contract manufacturer (an "assembly house", an EMS provider)
SMT: One of the processes used to make a PCBA — surface-mount technology, parts placed and reflowed on the surface. · The same assembly house

The confusion is not cosmetic. It decides who can quote you: a board house cannot assemble, and an assembly house that does not fabricate must buy the bare board from someone. When a supplier says "we do PCB and PCBA", ask which of the two happens in their building.

### What an actual PCBA order contains

Assembly starts from three files. Everything else is a refinement:

File: What it tells the factory
Gerber (RS-274X or ODB++): The physical board — copper, mask, paste layers, panelisation
BOM with manufacturer part numbers: What to buy, in what package, per reference designator
Centroid / pick-and-place: Where each part goes, at what rotation, on which side

Useful additions: stackup drawing for controlled impedance, test-point list, firmware binary, and any approved alternates. A quote built without a BOM is a guess about material cost, and material is usually the largest line on it.

### Which processes count as part of PCBA

A full-scope assembly house covers all of these in one building. Many cover only the first two:

- Solder paste printing and 3D SPI (paste volume, height, area, offset)
- SMT placement and reflow
- AOI after reflow, and X-ray on BGA/QFN joints that optics cannot see
- Through-hole insertion and wave or selective soldering
- Hand and post soldering for connectors, shields and heavy terminals
- Conformal coating, potting and underfill
- Depanelling and device programming with checksum binding
- Box build, harness, kitting and retail packing

Ask which of the eight happen on site. "We do turnkey" is not an answer to that question.

### What PCBA does not include

Two things are routinely assumed and routinely wrong:

- Bare-board fabrication. Many assembly houses, including ours, do not fabricate. Boards are purchased from qualified partner fabs and inspected on arrival. That is a supply choice, not a quality shortcut — but you should know which model you are buying.
- Electrical test. SPI, AOI and X-ray prove that solder joints are formed correctly. They do not prove the board works. In-circuit test (ICT) and functional test (FCT) are a separate purchase, and a plant can legitimately be excellent at assembly and not own a tester.

If a supplier's answer to "do you test it?" is "we inspect 100%", they have answered a different question.

### How to tell an assembly house from a PCB house in one minute

Three questions, in this order:

- "Do you fabricate the bare board, or buy it?" Either answer can be fine. An unclear answer is not.
- "What is your finest placement pitch, on which machine, on which line?" A capability claim without a machine and a line assignment is marketing.
- "Which operations in your process are subcontracted?" Every plant subcontracts something. A plant that says "nothing" is not answering.

### Where we sit in this split

We are an assembly house, not a PCB fabricator, and we say so first. Eight Yamaha YSM20/YSM10 lines, 01005 to 0.30 mm pitch, boards to 800 × 480 mm double-sided, in-line 3D SPI, AOI and X-ray on every shift, with through-hole, selective solder, conformal coating, programming and box build in the same building. Minimum order 50 pieces, three working days from kitted parts.

Bare boards come from qualified partner fabs. In-circuit and functional test are not in the building — they run through a qualified partner and are quoted as their own line. Both facts are on capabilities.html (/capabilities.html), because a buyer who finds out at tooling stage has been misled by omission.

The step-by-step version of the process is on assembly.html (/assembly.html). If your next question is what the assembly step costs, what is inside a PCBA price (/insights/pcba-cost-per-board.html) breaks it into five lines.

## Consigned vs turnkey PCBA at 50, 500 and 5,000 pieces

Source: https://tenmaypcba.com/insights/consigned-vs-turnkey-pcba.html
Published: 2026-11-16
Summary: Consigning is cheaper only when you already own the parts. The flip point is driven by purchasing labour and shortage risk, not by the assembly unit price.

The short answer: consigning is cheaper when you already own the parts or can buy them at a genuine contract price; turnkey is cheaper when your own purchasing time costs more than the margin the factory adds. The flip point usually sits somewhere between 500 and a few thousand pieces, and it is driven by three costs, not by the unit price of the assembly.

Below is where each cost sits, what it does at 50, 500 and 5,000 pieces, and the four questions that decide it for a specific build.

### The three costs that actually move

Cost: Who carries it · At 50 pcs · At 500 pcs · At 5,000 pcs
Component price: Whoever buys · Small order quantities rarely reach a contract price; reel minimums and cut-tape premiums bite hardest here · Distributor break quantities start to work in your favour · Only a genuine contract price or an OEM allocation beats the factory's franchised channel
Purchasing labour: Your team, if consigning · A BOM of a few hundred lines takes real hours to quote, buy, receive and kit — at 50 pcs this labour is spread over very few boards · Labour is the same, spread over more boards · Labour per board becomes negligible either way
Shortage and line-stop risk: Whoever buys · One missing line stops a small build completely; a factory carrying the kit usually has an approved alternate · Moderate — a shortage list still costs a week · Highest absolute exposure: a stopped line at this volume is expensive

Two more costs sit underneath those three and are easy to forget:

- Incoming inspection. Consigned parts still have to be counted, checked for date code and provenance, and dried if moisture-sensitive. If your factory does not log this, you find out at reflow, not at goods-in.
- Cash and storage. Consigning moves inventory onto your balance sheet and into your warehouse. At 5,000 pcs that is a real carrying cost, not a footnote.

### Three decision rules

Rule 1 — If you already hold the parts, consign them.
Stock on your shelf has already been paid for. Sending it to be assembled converts dead inventory into finished boards; buying it again through a factory is buying the same part twice.

Rule 2 — If the BOM has more than roughly a hundred lines and the batch is under 500, take turnkey.
The purchasing labour per board is the dominant term at that size. A shortage list from the factory within one working day is cheaper than your buyer spending three days chasing three lines.

Rule 3 — If a single part is on allocation, split the model.
Consign the allocated part, let the factory buy the rest. This is the case partial turnkey exists for, and it keeps the shortage risk with the party that already owns the constraint.

### What each model asks you to send

Model: You send · You keep · What changes in the quote
Full turnkey: Gerber, BOM, centroid · Nothing but the approval · Quote includes BOM pass-through and alternates approval
Partial turnkey: Gerber, BOM, centroid, plus the long-lead parts · The constrained lines · Quote splits: your consigned lines excluded, rest pass-through
Consigned kit: Gerber, BOM, centroid and the full kit · Everything · Quote is assembly plus tooling only; incoming check is against your BOM line by line

At Tenmay all three run on the same lines at the same minimum — fifty pieces — so the model is a commercial choice, not a scheduling one.

### Four questions that settle it for a specific build

- Do we already own the parts, or are we about to buy them? If ownership is already there, the comparison is not "our price vs factory price", it is "assembly cost vs doing nothing with the stock".
- How many BOM lines, and how many of them are single-source? Line count drives your labour; single-source lines drive the shortage risk.
- What is one week of delay worth on this product? This is the number most buyers never write down, and it is usually larger than the component margin being argued over.
- Who is checking provenance? Franchised vs broker is a quality decision before it is a price decision. If the parts are consigned, that decision is yours and it should be documented.

### The mistake that costs the most

Comparing the two models on unit price only. Turnkey's margin and consigning's labour cost are both visible; the shortage risk, the incoming inspection and the carrying cost are not. A build quoted a few percent cheaper on consigned parts can lose that advantage in the first line stop.

If the two quotes are within a few percent, choose the model that puts the shortage risk with the party that can see the stock position daily.

### FAQ

### Is consigning always cheaper for small batches?

No. It is cheaper when you already own the parts. If you have to buy them anyway, the purchasing labour at 50 pcs usually outweighs the component margin a factory would add.

### Can we switch model between the first run and the re-order?

Yes, and it is common: consign the first build from existing stock, then move to turnkey once volumes justify a purchasing cycle. The Gerber and BOM revision stay the same, so no new NRE applies at Tenmay on an unchanged revision.

### Who pays for parts damaged in assembly?

It depends on the cause, and this must be written into the PO: incoming material faults belong to the consigning party, process faults to the assembler. This is one of the four terms buyers most often leave out.

### Does the model change the lead time?

Only through the kit. Tenmay's standard lead time is three days once the kit is complete — a consigned kit that arrives short simply moves the start date, it does not move the build duration.

Written by the Tenmay assembly engineering team. No customer names and no yield percentages are published: we do not have permission to publish them, and an invented number would be worse than none. Batch sizes in the table are the ranges the plant is scheduled around; component pricing is not published because it moves with allocation and market conditions.

## The four clocks inside a PCBA lead time

Source: https://tenmaypcba.com/insights/four-clocks-in-a-pcba-lead-time.html
Published: 2026-11-16
Summary: Build time, material time, engineering time and transit time are four different waits. Quoting one number for the four is how delivery promises break.

"The build is three days" and "you will have boards in three days" are different statements, and treating them as the same one is the most common reason a first order arrives late. Four clocks run at once. Only one of them is the assembly floor's to shorten.

### Clock one — the build

This is the short one. Once the parts are kitted, the stencil is cut, the programme is loaded and the first article has been approved, a standard run on this floor is three working days. Panel count, not board count, sets the shape of that: a small board that panels up well is quick, a board near the 800 × 480 mm limit is fewer per pass and slower per unit.

The build clock is the one a supplier can control, and the one buyers tend to quote to their own customers. That is the mistake.

### Clock two — the material

Component lead time is usually the real date. Two boards with identical process difficulty can be six weeks apart because of one part: a connector on allocation, an MCU in a specific package, a capacitor with a long-life specification that only one series meets.

Practical rules:

- Long-lead parts decide the schedule, not the average part. Ask which line on the BOM is the critical path before the order is placed, not after.
- A broker part shortens the clock and lengthens the risk. Same part number, unknown storage history. It is a legitimate choice for a prototype and a bad one for a production run.
- Consigned material moves the clock to you. The floor cannot start until the box arrives and has been counted and checked against the BOM. Shipping a partial kit does not start a partial build.

### Clock three — the engineering

Engineering is not a queue you wait in; it is a set of questions that must be answered before the line starts. Paste apertures on a fine-pitch part, panelisation and breakaway, fiducial position, polarity, coating mask. Each one is small. Each one, unanswered, stops the run.

This clock is the most compressible, and the only way to compress it is to answer early. A DFM review returned before the parts are ordered costs a day. The same question discovered at setup costs a week and a stencil.

### Clock four — transit

Ex-works is not delivered. Air freight from Shenzhen to Europe or North America is days; sea is weeks; and the customs end has its own variability that no factory can quote. If a delivery date matters, it should be stated as a door date with the transit assumption written next to it, so the day the assumption changes is visible to both sides.

### Putting the four together

Clock: Who controls it · What shortens it
Build: The assembly floor · Kitted parts, approved first article, unchanged revision
Material: Distributor and allocation · Earlier BOM freeze, approved alternatives, avoiding broker stock
Engineering: Both sides · DFM answered before the parts order
Transit: Carrier and customs · Correct paperwork; mode chosen deliberately, not by default

A realistic date is the longest of the first three plus the fourth. When someone quotes a single number, the useful question is which clock they are quoting — and whether the answer includes the material.

### Why the reorder is faster

On a reorder with the same revision, clock two and clock three are already paid: parts are known, the stencil and programme exist, the first article is approved. What remains is material availability and the build. That is why the second order behaves differently from the first, and why a supplier who keeps your setup files is worth more than a supplier who is slightly cheaper on the first run.

---

## What a DFM review catches before the stencil is cut

Source: https://tenmaypcba.com/insights/dfm-review-before-the-stencil.html
Published: 2026-11-15
Summary: A DFM review is not a courtesy. It is the last point where a change costs a file edit rather than a stencil, a scrap batch or a hand-rework line.

Design for manufacture is usually described as a set of rules. In practice it is a set of decisions with deadlines. Every check below is cheap while the design is a file, expensive once a stencil exists, and unrecoverable once a batch has been built.

### The ten checks, in the order they bite

1. Aperture and pad geometry against the smallest part. A 01005 chip and a 0.3 mm-pitch IC do not share a paste strategy. Apertures that suit one starve or bridge the other. This is the check that most often produces a design change, because it is a drawing edit rather than a component change.

2. Panelisation and breakaway. How the board is arrayed decides how many fit through the line per pass, whether the assembly can be depanelised without stressing joints, and where the fiducials go. A board can be perfectly designed and panel badly: mouse-bites in the wrong place, no rail to clamp, tooling holes absent.

3. Fiducials and local references. Global fiducials for the panel, local ones for fine-pitch parts. Missing references mean the machine places by board outline and the accuracy you paid for is not used.

4. Component orientation and polarity. Diode and electrolytic polarity marked unambiguously on the silkscreen, pin 1 marked on every multi-pin package. A board with ambiguous orientation will eventually be built wrong, and the rework is a hand operation.

5. Courtyard and spacing. Parts placed so the nozzle can reach them and the reflow air can move around them. Two tall components side by side shadow each other; a part against a tall connector cannot be placed after it.

6. Thermal balance. Large copper pours and thick ground planes pull heat out of a joint. A board with a heavy plane on one side and fine-pitch parts on the other needs a profile developed for it, not a default one. This shows up as a yield problem rather than a design error, which is why it is worth naming early.

7. Through-hole and mixed technology. Which side the through-hole parts sit on decides whether the process is pin-in-paste, selective solder or hand. Each is a different line and a different price, and the choice is usually fixable in the layout.

8. Coating and masking. If conformal coating is specified, connectors, test points, optical surfaces and any press-fit area need to be maskable. Masking is hand labour; a design that scatters unmaskable features across the board turns a cheap step into an expensive one.

9. Test access. Test points large enough and reachable, with the plane under them clear. If functional test happens at your end, the fixture needs access that the layout must provide.

10. BOM reality. Manufacturer part numbers that exist, packages that match the footprint, and alternatives named where a part is single-source. A BOM with a package mismatch is found at kitting, which is the most expensive possible moment.

### Which of these change the price

Three do, directly: panelisation (units per pass), through-hole method (line and labour), and coating masking (hand labour). The rest change the risk rather than the price, which is harder to see on a quote and easier to see on the third delivery.

### What a review cannot do

It cannot make a design good. It can make it buildable. A DFM review that returns "no issues" is not a statement that the product works — only that the file can be manufactured as drawn.

It also cannot replace the first article. The first board off the line is checked against the drawing, and that check is the point where a DFM assumption meets a real stencil and a real paste deposit.

### How to get a useful review

Send the Gerber with the drill file, the BOM with manufacturer part numbers, the centroid file, and the quantity. State the coating and the test plan. Then ask one question: what in this design will cost me money at setup? The answer is a shorter list than a full DFM report, and it is the list that decides the quote.

We review every file before quoting, in-house, and we return the findings as questions rather than as a verdict. Where the answer is that a process is not run here — full functional test with a load bank, for example — that is stated before the order rather than after the first batch.

---

## Why the second run costs less than the first — and where that stops

Source: https://tenmaypcba.com/insights/why-the-second-run-costs-less.html
Published: 2026-11-14
Summary: A reorder is cheaper because the fixed work is already done, not because the supplier likes you. Four things must stay unchanged for that to hold.

On a fifty-piece run, the one-time work is a large share of the unit price. On the same job a second time, most of it has already been paid. That is the whole mechanism — and it has conditions. When one of the conditions breaks, the saving disappears and buyers are usually surprised by how completely.

### What carries over

Item: Carried over · What can cancel it
Stencil: Yes, while the apertures are unchanged · Any change to pad geometry, or a worn stencil past its usable life
SMT programme: Yes, while the placement data is unchanged · Moving a part, changing a package, or a rotated footprint
Reflow profile: Yes, while the board construction is unchanged · Layer count, copper weight, or a large change in thermal mass
First-article approval: Yes, for the same revision · Any revision change, or a long gap that triggers a re-qualification
Kitting knowledge: Partly · A BOM change, or a part that was sourced from a specific distributor
Setup and changeover: No · Charged again on every run, because the line is reconfigured either way

The last row is the one buyers misread. Setup is not a one-time charge that disappears on a reorder; changeover happens every time the line starts your job. What disappears is the engineering — the stencil, the programme, the profile development, the first article.

### The four things that must stay unchanged

Same revision. One resistor value change is enough to require a new stencil check, a re-verification of the programme and a fresh first article. It may be a ten-minute change at your desk and a re-qualification at the factory.

Same process. Switching a board from a single-sided to a double-sided build, or adding conformal coating, changes the routing, not just the price.

Same supplier. This is the honest one. Your stencil, programme and profile live with the factory that built the job. Moving to a cheaper supplier resets the engineering clock to zero, which is why a supplier switch on a mature product often costs more in the first order than it saves in the second.

Same or equivalent material. If a component goes on allocation, the reorder can be blocked at kitting even though nothing about the board changed. Naming an approved alternative on the BOM is the cheapest insurance available.

### Where the saving stops

Two limits are worth stating before a buyer plans around them.

Volume. Below roughly fifty pieces the setup and first-article work dominates, and the reorder saving is proportionally large. Above a few thousand pieces a month, a dedicated high-volume line with cheaper hourly rates starts to win on unit price, and the reorder advantage of a high-mix floor stops being the deciding factor.

Product life. A board that is revised twice a year never reaches the cheap state. The reorder saving assumes a design that has settled, and part of the value of a DFM review is getting a design to that state before the first order rather than after the third.

### What to ask for on a reorder quote

Ask for three things in writing: whether the stencil is still in usable condition, whether the programme and profile are the current revision, and whether any line on the BOM has moved to allocation since the last run. Those three answers determine whether the second price is a real reduction or an optimism.

We keep tooling and setup files against the customer's revision, and we quote the reorder against the same revision that was built. When a revision changes, the reorder is quoted as a first run, because that is what it is.

---

## 01005 vs 0201: which package should your design use?

Source: https://tenmaypcba.com/insights/01005-vs-0201.html
Published: 2026-11-07
Summary: The gap is 0.2 mm in each direction and a measurable defect rate. Use the largest package the layout allows, and go smaller only when the board forces it.

01005 measures 0.4 x 0.2 mm and 0201 measures 0.6 x 0.3 mm. The difference is 0.2 mm in each direction — and in production it is the difference between a routine part and one that eats yield. Use the largest package the layout allows; specify 01005 only when board area or signal integrity forces it.

### First, a naming trap worth clearing up

Package codes are imperial, in hundredths of an inch. That means "0201" is 0.02 x 0.01 inch, which converts to 0.6 x 0.3 mm. The metric name for the same part is 0603 — which collides with the imperial 0603 (1.6 x 0.8 mm).

So a BOM that says "0603" is ambiguous unless the standard is stated. Ask which one you are getting before the stencil is cut. This single confusion causes more re-quotes than any other line on a BOM.

### How the common sizes compare

Imperial: Metric · Size (mm) · Placement · Stencil aperture · Typical use
0402: 1005 · 1.0 x 0.5 · Routine · Comfortable · Default for most boards
0201: 0603 · 0.6 x 0.3 · Standard, needs good paste · Tight · Dense consumer, modules
01005: 0402 · 0.4 x 0.2 · Demanding · Near area-ratio limit · Wearables, implantable, space-critical

### What actually gets harder at 01005

The placement machine is rarely the limit. Four other things are:

- Paste volume. The stencil aperture becomes small enough that the aperture's area-to-wall-area ratio decides whether paste releases at all. This pushes toward thinner stencils and finer paste classification.
- Tombstoning and skew. Less solder, less self-alignment force during reflow. The part has to land right rather than being pulled right.
- Handling. Parts this size are difficult to rework by hand, so a single defect is often a scrap decision rather than a repair.
- Inspection. Optical inspection needs enough contrast and resolution to judge a fillet measured in tens of microns.

None of these are reasons to avoid 01005. They are reasons to pay for them only when the design earns it.

### When is 0201 the better answer?

Almost always, unless one of these is true:

- The board is area-constrained — a module, a wearable, an implant, where the enclosure is the requirement.
- Loop inductance matters — decoupling placed closer to the pin, which is a real electrical reason, not a cosmetic one.
- The assembly is already dense — if you are at 0.3 mm IC pitch, the passives are no longer the hardest thing on the board.

If none apply, moving from 0201 to 0402 usually lowers cost and defect rate without changing function. That is a design decision worth making explicitly rather than inheriting from a reference design.

### What to confirm with the manufacturer before you commit

- Can they place it, and on which line? A capability claim without a line assignment is not a commitment.
- What paste and stencil combination do they use for it?
- What is their first-article process for a package this size — is it inspected optically, by X-ray, or both?

At Shenzhen Tenmay Technology the placement floor runs down to 01005 on Yamaha YSM20/YSM10 lines with in-line SPI, AOI and X-ray, and the capabilities page (/capabilities.html) states the 0.3 mm pitch and 800 x 480 mm board limits that decide whether a design fits. If your question is about yield at that size rather than package choice, this note on 01005 yield limits (/insights/01005-placement-what-limits-yield.html) goes through the stencil and paste side in more detail.

Last reviewed: 2026-11-17 · Send the BOM and Gerber for a DFM read: WhatsApp (https://wa.me/8617361058693)

## What SPI, AOI and X-ray can catch — and what they cannot

Source: https://tenmaypcba.com/insights/what-aoi-xray-cannot-catch.html
Published: 2026-11-07
Summary: SPI checks paste, AOI checks what is visible, X-ray checks what is hidden. None of them checks whether the board works — and knowing the gap is what makes an inspection claim meaningful.

SPI verifies solder paste before placement. AOI verifies visible features after reflow — presence, polarity, offset, fillet shape. X-ray verifies joints hidden under packages, especially BGA and QFN. None of the three verifies electrical function, and none replaces a functional test.

### What each station is actually proving

Station: When it inspects · What it proves · What it cannot see
SPI: After paste print, before placement · Paste volume, height, area, offset per pad · Anything about the component or the joint
AOI: After reflow · Presence, polarity, rotation, offset, fillet shape, bridging · Anything under a package or in shadow
X-ray: After reflow · Voids, bridging, head-in-pillow, ball collapse under BGA/QFN · Component presence, value, or function

The useful reading of that table: the three stations cover three different moments, not three levels of the same check.

### Where defects actually get through

Optical inspection is a contrast problem before it is an algorithm problem. These are the recurring blind spots:

- Black component on black solder mask. Low contrast means a marginal offset can pass.
- Anything under a package. AOI is line-of-sight; a BGA joint is not in the line of sight. This is precisely why X-ray exists.
- Shadowed joints on a dense board. Tall components cast occlusion; an inspector or an algorithm sees the top of the shadow, not the joint.
- Solder voids below the reporting threshold. X-ray will show a void; whether it matters is a specification question, not a detection question.
- Wrong value, right package. A 10 kΩ resistor substituted for a 1 kΩ one looks identical. No optical or X-ray station catches this — only electrical test or incoming verification does.
- Weak or cold joints that are still shaped correctly. A joint can be visually acceptable and electrically intermittent.

That last row is the one that costs money in the field, because it passes every inspection station and fails in the customer's hands.

### So what closes the gap?

Three things that are not inspection:

- In-circuit test or flying probe — proves connectivity and component values.
- Functional test — proves the assembly does what it is for, under power.
- Boundary scan — reaches nets that probing cannot touch.

A program that claims "full inspection" and stops at AOI has covered placement, not function. A program that claims "100% tested" needs to say which of the three above it means. On a dense board with 0.3 mm pitch, the difference between the three is the difference between a joint check and a function check.

### What a supplier should be able to tell you

- Which stations run in line, and on which products — not which machines are owned. A line that inspects a 5,000 pcs batch is not necessarily inspecting every board in it.
- What the first-article process is, and who signs it off.
- What happens to a board that fails AOI: rework, re-inspect, or scrap — and whether rework is re-inspected at the same station.
- Whether functional test exists for your product, and who writes the fixture.

If the answer to the last one is "the customer tests it", then the inspection claim covers assembly only. That is a legitimate arrangement — it just needs to be stated, because the buyer's risk sits after the point where the supplier stopped looking.

### Why this matters commercially

Inspection claims are easy to inflate and hard to audit. A manufacturer that says "we have AOI and X-ray" has told you about equipment. One that says "we catch placement defects optically, hidden joints by X-ray, and connectivity by flying probe — but not component value drift over temperature" has told you where your risk is.

Shenzhen Tenmay Technology runs SPI, AOI and X-ray in line on its Yamaha YSM20/YSM10 lines; the assembly page (/assembly.html) describes where each station sits in the flow, and capabilities (/capabilities.html) lists the equipment. Electrical test is quoted per project rather than claimed as standard, because the fixture is product-specific.

## What is HMLV in PCBA — and when does it cost more than high volume?

Source: https://tenmaypcba.com/insights/what-is-hmlv-pcba.html
Published: 2026-11-07
Summary: HMLV is a production model, not a batch size. The cost difference comes from setup amortisation and changeover time, and both can be measured.

HMLV stands for high-mix, low-volume. It describes a production model where a factory runs many different products in small batches, rather than one product in large batches. The cost of HMLV comes from setup and changeover being repeated far more often; the benefit is that a small order can be built at all.

### Is HMLV a quantity, or a model?

It is a model, and quantity is only one signal of it. The defining feature is how often the line stops and reconfigures. A factory building eighty different assemblies a month in batches of fifty is HMLV. A factory building one assembly in batches of fifty thousand is not, even though some of its individual orders are small.

The practical consequence: HMLV work is priced on reconfiguration, not on board area. If you ask for a quote and the reply is built from square centimetres and component count, it is a high-volume quote wearing a small-batch hat.

### Where the extra cost actually sits

Four activities repeat once per order rather than once per batch of ten thousand:

Activity: When it happens · Scales with quantity?
Stencil fabrication: Once per assembly revision · No
Machine programming and feeder setup: Once per assembly · No
First-article inspection and sign-off: Once per assembly · No
Component kitting and verification: Once per order · Partly

Add changeover — unloading the previous product's feeders and loading the next — and you have the whole difference. Solder, components and placement time per board are close to identical between a fifty-piece run and a fifty-thousand-piece run.

### So how much more does a small batch cost per board?

The arithmetic is simple once the fixed part is known. Suppose a setup consumes 4 hours of line time before the first board is placed. Spread over 50 pcs, that is 4.8 minutes of setup per board. Over 5,000 pcs, it is 2.9 seconds.

That is the entire mechanic. The percentage uplift depends on how much assembly time each board needs — a dense board with two hundred placements dilutes setup faster than a simple one — which is why a per-board price quoted without knowing the batch size is guesswork.

### When does HMLV not cost more?

Three cases:

- When the product never changes. If the same assembly repeats every month, the stencil and programme are already on file, and only the kitting repeats. The fixed cost has effectively been paid.
- When volume would create inventory you cannot sell. A ten-thousand-piece run halves the unit price and doubles the capital tied up in finished goods. For a product with uncertain demand, the cheaper unit price is the more expensive decision.
- When the design is still moving. Re-running a large batch after an engineering change is the most expensive outcome in this business. Small batches absorb revisions.

### What to ask a supplier to find out which one you are buying

- Which of the setup steps are charged separately, and which are absorbed?
- Is there a price break, and at what quantity does it start?
- If the same assembly is reordered next quarter, what does the second run cost compared with the first?

That last question separates a genuine HMLV operation from one that simply tolerates small orders at a penalty. A factory set up for mixed production keeps the programme and the stencil, so a repeat order should not pay the full setup again.

### What this looks like on a real line

At the Shenzhen facility of Shenzhen Tenmay Technology, high-mix work is the normal case: eight Yamaha YSM20/YSM10 lines, batches from 50 pcs, and feeder carts loaded per order. The visible cost of HMLV is the kitting bench — the reels being loaded in the photograph above — because that is where changeover becomes labour.

If you want the process side of this rather than the commercial side, the assembly (/assembly.html) page covers what runs in line, and capabilities (/capabilities.html) lists the placement limits that decide whether your design fits a small-batch line at all.

Last reviewed: 2026-11-17 · Send the BOM and Gerber for a DFM read: WhatsApp (https://wa.me/8617361058693)

## What actually limits 01005 placement yield?

Source: https://tenmaypcba.com/insights/01005-placement-what-limits-yield.html
Published: 2026-11-06
Summary: The placer is rarely the constraint. Stencil, paste, pad geometry and inspection each cap what a 01005 design can do on a real line.

The placement head is almost never the limit. A 01005 part is about 0.4 × 0.2 mm, and every current placer can position it. What caps yield is how much solder the stencil releases, which paste carries it, whether the pads hold it centred, and whether inspection can see the joint at all.

### Is the placement machine the limit?

No, and treating it as the limit leads to the wrong fixes. A board that places cleanly and still fails at reflow or at AOI is showing a paste-volume problem, not a positioning problem. Turning up placement accuracy cannot deposit more solder.

At this size the process stops being about positioning and starts being about deposit — how much solder lands on the pad, and how much of it stays where it was put.

### What does the stencil set?

Paste release is the first ceiling. For a 01005 land the aperture is small enough that the area ratio — aperture opening area against the area of its walls — decides whether paste leaves the stencil at all.

When that ratio falls too low, paste stays in the aperture and releases unevenly. It looks like a placement defect: parts tombstone, pull to one pad, or end up with too little solder on one side. Changing placer settings will not fix any of those.

Lever: What it buys · What it costs
Thinner stencil foil: Better area ratio at the same aperture · Less paste volume for the larger parts sharing the panel
Laser-cut or electroformed apertures: Cleaner wall finish, more consistent release · Higher stencil cost per revision
Aperture geometry adjusted to the land, not copied from it: A centred deposit · Time at the DFM stage
Nano-coating on the foil: Release when a thin foil is not an option · Consumable cost per stencil

### Which paste type does 01005 need?

Type 3 paste in a 01005 aperture is a volume problem before it is a printing problem. Type 4 is the usual answer, and Type 5 appears where apertures are smaller still.

Paste type: Where it fits · Trade-off
Type 3: 0402 and larger · Will not reliably fill a 01005 aperture
Type 4: 01005 alongside 0402 and above · The normal compromise on mixed panels
Type 5: Apertures below the 01005 window · Finer powder oxidises faster and shortens stencil life

The compromise is worth stating plainly: a Type 5 paste left on the stencil across a long run behaves worse than a Type 4 paste refreshed on schedule. On a mixed panel the paste choice is made for the whole board, not for the smallest part alone.

### Which pad and mask choices cause 01005 defects?

Two layout decisions cause most of the avoidable defects, and a third is quieter:

Layout choice: What happens at 01005 · What to do instead
Solder-mask-defined land: Effective copper area shrinks and the deposit becomes unpredictable · Copper-defined land with a mask dam
Via-in-pad without fill: Paste wicks into the via; the part sits low or drifts · Fill and cap the via at fabrication, or move it out of the land
Asymmetric copper around the two pads: Uneven thermal mass pulls the part toward the hotter side · Balance copper on both pads

The third one is survivable at 0402 and a tombstone at 01005. It is a layout fix, and it is decided before the files ever reach an assembly floor.

### Where does the placer still matter?

Placement force and nozzle choice are where the machine earns its place. Too much force embeds the part in the paste and squeezes it sideways; too little leaves it sitting on top, and reflow pulls it off-centre. Vacuum nozzles sized to the part, with force set low, are the normal configuration.

Vision also needs clean contrast between part and background. Black parts on dark tape, or parts with a mirror finish, occasionally need a different lighting recipe. That is a per-part setup item, not a per-board one — which is exactly why high-mix work carries setup cost a single-product line never sees.

### What can inspection actually verify at 01005?

This is the part most capability tables skip. A line can place 01005 and still not be able to verify it.

Optical inspection at this scale depends on resolution and on how much shadow the neighbouring components cast. A board with tall electrolytics beside 01005 passives has blind angles. X-ray helps with joints under area-array parts, but it is not a substitute for optical inspection of passives — the solder volume is small and the contrast is poor.

So the accurate claim is narrower than "we place 01005". It is: we place 01005, we inspect it optically where the neighbouring geometry allows, and we tell you which areas of your board fall outside that.

### What we will not claim

- No pass-yield percentage for 01005 on your design before the stencil and pad geometry have been reviewed.
- No blanket "100% inspected" statement: optical coverage depends on component height around the part.
- No quoting a 01005 build from a BOM alone. The stencil drawing and the land pattern decide whether the job is routine or engineering-reviewed.

### What to send with a 01005 enquiry

Three things decide whether the quote is realistic:

- The paste type the design assumes, or the smallest aperture on the stencil drawing.
- Whether any 01005 land has via-in-pad beneath it.
- How many 01005 parts sit next to tall components, since that decides inspectability.

Send the Gerber, the BOM and the centroid, and ask for a DFM note specifically on the 01005 areas. The capabilities page (/capabilities.html) lists the placement window we hold today — 01005 passives, 0.3 mm minimum IC pitch, boards up to 800 × 480 mm — and the assembly page (/assembly.html) shows where in-line SPI, AOI and X-ray sit in the flow. A supplier who answers a DFM note in writing tells you more than any capability table.

If the package choice is still open, 01005 vs 0201 (/insights/01005-vs-0201.html) sets out when the smaller part is actually necessary, and what AOI and X-ray can and cannot catch (/insights/what-aoi-xray-cannot-catch.html) explains the inspection gap in more detail.

Last reviewed: 2026-11-17 · Send the BOM and Gerber for a DFM read: WhatsApp (https://wa.me/8617361058693)

## Which BOM problems force a re-quote — and how do you catch them first?

Source: https://tenmaypcba.com/insights/bom-substitution-checklist.html
Published: 2026-11-06
Summary: A BOM that reads correctly can still be unbuyable. These eight checks decide whether the parts arrive as listed or the job stops for approval.

Eight checks cover almost every substitution that stops a job: lifecycle status, a real second source, electrical margins, package and polarity, moisture sensitivity, packaging format, order multiple, and date-code provenance. A BOM that passes all eight can be bought as written, which means no approval loop and no price movement before assembly starts.

### What is a re-quote, and why does it cost time?

A re-quote is what happens when procurement cannot buy the BOM as written. The part number exists, the quantity is right, the reference designators all match — and then the exact part turns out to be on a lead that runs to 90 days, sold only in reels of 5,000 pcs, or marked obsolete.

At that point the job stops. Someone proposes an alternative, someone else approves it, and the price may move. Nearly all of it is avoidable with a pass through the BOM before the enquiry is sent.

### The eight checks, on one page

#: Check · What goes wrong when it fails
1: Lifecycle status · An end-of-life part is available this build and gone the next; the replacement was never qualified
2: Real second source · "Or equivalent" moves the decision to whoever is buying, which is the wrong place for it
3: Electrical margins · The substitute matches the headline value and fails two lines down on tolerance, rating or thermal drift
4: Package, land and polarity · Same footprint, different pin function — or a part placed the wrong way round
5: Moisture sensitivity level · A higher MSL adds baking and a floor-life clock nobody planned for
6: Packaging format · Cut tape that cannot be fed turns machine placement into hand placement
7: Order multiple · A part sold in reels of 5,000 pcs for a build that consumes 50 pcs
8: Date code and provenance · Old material or open-market stock goes into a product with a warranty

### 1. Is the part still active?

Lifecycle status is the first check and the cheapest. A part marked end-of-life or not-recommended-for-new-designs will stop being available eventually, and the version on the next build may not be the one you qualified.

Distributor product pages usually carry status. Checking the twenty highest-value lines catches most of the problem, because that is where the cost and the risk sit.

### 2. Is there a real second source?

Two different things get called a second source, and only one helps:

- An alternate manufacturer's part number, listed with its own MPN. Useful — it can be bought directly.
- The phrase "or equivalent". Not useful on its own. It hands the decision to the buyer at the factory, who has no visibility of why the part was chosen.

If a line must not be substituted — a specific regulator, a matched pair, an MCU with calibrated internals — say so explicitly. Silence reads as permission.

### 3. Do the electrical parameters actually match?

The common failure is a substitution that is right on the headline spec and wrong in the detail. Before approving an alternate, check:

Parameter: What to compare, not just copy
Tolerance and temperature coefficient: Nominal value, then drift over the operating range
Voltage rating: Include the derating margin the design assumes
Package and pinout: Same footprint does not always mean same pin function
Timing or frequency: Anything with a crystal or oscillator
Operating temperature range: An industrial part swapped for a commercial one is a field failure waiting to ship

### 4. Does the land pattern and polarity carry over?

A 0402 part is not always the same 0402 land. Check the alternate manufacturer's recommended land pattern instead of assuming the footprint transfers. For anything with polarity — diodes, tantalum capacitors, electrolytics, LEDs — check that the marking orientation matches the assembly drawing.

This is where a substitution becomes a silent defect: the board builds, passes basic inspection, and fails in the field because the part went on the wrong way round.

### 5. Did the moisture sensitivity level change?

An alternate with a higher MSL changes the handling requirement. It may need baking before use, and it has a floor-life limit once the seal is broken.

If the original was MSL 1 and the alternate is MSL 3, the process has changed even though the part-number swap looked trivial. Tell the assembler, or they find out at reflow.

### 6. Is the packaging feedable?

Quantity is not packaging. A part quoted as cut tape may arrive as loose pieces that cannot be fed automatically, which turns machine placement into hand placement and moves the price.

Packaging: Effect on a small build
Full reel: Feedable, but may carry an order multiple far above usage
Partial reel or feedable cut length: The practical option for small runs; ask for it explicitly
Loose cut tape: Usually hand placement, and a price change
Tray or tube: Fine for the parts designed for it; not interchangeable with reel

For small runs, this single item causes more price movement than any other line in the BOM.

### 7. What is the order multiple?

A line needing 50 pcs of a part sold in reels of 5,000 pcs is a purchasing decision, not a pricing detail. Decide in advance how the balance is handled: bought and stocked, consigned by you, or avoided by choosing a part with a smaller multiple. The material-policy section of why a 50-piece run costs more per board (/insights/fifty-piece-run-cost.html) sets out the three options.

### 8. Is the date code and provenance on record?

For anything going into a product with a warranty, the age of the material matters. Ask what date-code policy applies and whether parts come from authorised distribution or the open market.

Open-market sourcing is legitimate, and sometimes the only option for an obsolete part. It is not the same as authorised stock, and the difference belongs on the record rather than discovered later.

### What four columns make a BOM survive procurement?

Add these to a normal BOM and most of the back-and-forth disappears:

- Approved alternates, each with a real manufacturer part number.
- Substitution rule per line: exact where nothing may change, equivalent where a matching spec is acceptable.
- Critical parameters for lines marked equivalent — the two or three numbers that must match.
- Notes for anything with a handling constraint, a polarity quirk or a matched pair.

Small work at design time, and it removes an entire class of delay at build time.

### What we will not do

- No silent substitution. Where a line cannot be bought as written, we say which line, what the options are, and the price effect of each.
- No approval after the fact. If a substitution needs sign-off, the run waits for it rather than shipping and explaining.
- No claim that an alternate is fully equivalent without the two or three critical parameters being named.

For a first enquiry we need the Gerber, the BOM and the centroid. If the BOM carries alternates and substitution rules, the DFM note comes back faster because there is less to ask about. The capabilities page (/capabilities.html) covers the component sourcing and CoC side — what we buy, what we verify on incoming material, and what we do not hold in-house.
